Identifies added operational complexity of the control plane

questions.title: Write an S3 Remote Backend With a DynamoDB Lock Table
questions.prompt: Write the Terraform backend configuration for storing state in an S3 bucket with versioning enabled, encrypted at rest, and locked using a DynamoDB table, for a production environment.
questions.modelAnswer: The key structural detail is that the backend bucket, its versioning, encryption, and the DynamoDB lock table cannot be created by the same Terraform configuration that uses them as its backend - that would be a circular dependency, since Terraform needs the backend to exist before it can even initialize. These resources get bootstrapped once, either by hand or by a separate, minimal bootstrap configuration with its own (often local, one-time) state, and everything else then points at them as a backend. Versioning on the bucket is what makes state recovery possible after a bad apply corrupts state - without it, a destructive write to state is permanent. encrypt plus kms_key_id ensures state, which often contains sensitive values in plain text (database passwords, connection strings resolved as outputs), is encrypted at rest with a customer-managed key rather than the default S3 key, giving control over key rotation and access policy. The DynamoDB table with a LockID hash key is the mechanism preventing two concurrent terraform apply runs from racing against the same state - Terraform writes a lock item before starting work and removes it after, and a second run attempting to start while the lock exists fails immediately with a clear 'state locked' error instead of silently corrupting state through a concurrent write.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I make sure junior engineers understand first is that you can't have this exact configuration's own apply create the bucket and lock table it's also using as its backend - that's a chicken-and-egg problem, so those get bootstrapped separately, once, often by hand or in a tiny one-off state nobody touches again after setup. Versioning on the bucket isn't optional for me on anything production - it's the only thing that saves you when an apply goes wrong and corrupts state, because you can roll back to a previous version of the state file. I always use a customer-managed KMS key rather than the default, because state files routinely have sensitive output values sitting in them in plain text, and I want control over who can decrypt that and how the key gets rotated. The DynamoDB table is what actually stops two people from running apply at the same time and stepping on each other's changes - Terraform writes a lock record before it starts and whoever's second just gets a clean error instead of a race condition silently writing garbage into state.
commonMistakes: Tries to create the backend bucket/table in the same configuration that uses them, causing a circular dependency
Omits bucket versioning, removing the ability to recover from a corrupted state write
Uses default encryption instead of a customer-managed KMS key for sensitive state content
Omits the DynamoDB lock table, risking concurrent-apply state corruption

Explains why backend resources must be bootstrapped outside the configuration using them
Explains the role of bucket versioning for state recovery
Explains the DynamoDB lock table's role in preventing concurrent-apply corruption

Explains the bootstrap/circular-dependency issue correctly

questions.title: Write a Versioned Module Call Against a Private Registry
questions.prompt: Write a Terraform module call that consumes a 'networking' module from a private registry, pinned to a safe version constraint, along with the required_providers block pinning the AWS provider version for the root configuration.
questions.modelAnswer: Three separate version pins are doing distinct jobs here, and conflating them is a common mistake. required_version pins the Terraform CLI version itself, protecting against a CLI upgrade introducing behavior changes the configuration wasn't tested against. The required_providers block pins the AWS provider to '~> 5.40', meaning any 5.x release equal to or above 5.40 is acceptable but 6.0 is not, which protects against an unreviewed provider major version introducing breaking resource schema changes. The module's own version = '~> 2.3' pins the registry module similarly - accepting 2.3.x and later 2.x patches and minors, but never silently jumping to a 3.x release that might change required inputs or outputs. Using the private registry source format (app.terraform.io/org/module/provider, or an equivalent private registry host) rather than a raw Git URL gives version resolution, a browsable module registry UI, and provider compatibility metadata that a bare Git source doesn't provide. The '~>' operator specifically allows patch and minor updates within the pinned major (or minor, depending on how many version segments are specified) version, which is the standard way to get bug fixes automatically while requiring a deliberate, reviewed action to adopt a breaking change.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat these three pins as three separate insurance policies. required_version locks the Terraform binary itself, so nobody's local CLI upgrade surprises the team with new behavior mid-sprint. The provider version pin, '~> 5.40', means I'll happily take any 5.40-or-later patch and minor automatically, but a 6.0 release - which almost certainly has breaking schema changes somewhere - requires someone to deliberately bump that number and review what changed. Same logic on the module pin, '~> 2.3' - patches and minors flow in without anyone doing anything, a major version bump is a reviewed, intentional upgrade. I always use the actual registry source format over a raw Git URL when one's available, because the registry gives me a browsable version history and compatibility info that a Git tag reference just doesn't. The pattern I actually enforce on teams is: never leave a version constraint blank and never use a bare '>= x' with no upper bound, because that's how you end up getting someone else's breaking change on your next terraform init with zero review.
commonMistakes: Omits version pinning on either the provider or the module, or uses an unbounded constraint
Conflates the Terraform CLI version pin with the provider or module version pin
Uses a raw Git source instead of the registry source format with no justification
Doesn't explain the behavior of the ~> operator correctly
keyPoints: Writes a correct required_version, required_providers, and module version pin
Correctly explains the ~> operator's patch/minor-only behavior
Distinguishes the three separate version pins and what each protects against
Uses the correct registry module source format

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes correct, complete Terraform code with all three pins
Correctly explains the ~> version constraint behavior
Explains what each of the three pins protects against

questions.title: Write an OPA/Conftest Policy Denying Public S3 Buckets in a Terraform Plan
questions.prompt: Write a Rego policy (for use with Conftest or OPA against a Terraform plan JSON export) that fails the check if any aws_s3_bucket resource in the plan has a public ACL.
questions.code:
package main

# Run with: terraform show -json plan.tfplan > plan.json && conftest test plan.json

deny[msg] {
  resource := input.resource_changes[_]
  resource.type == "aws_s3_bucket_acl"
  acl := resource.change.after.acl
  acl == "public-read"
  msg := sprintf("S3 bucket ACL '%s' on resource '%s' is public and not allowed", [acl, resource.address])
}

deny[msg] {
  resource := input.resource_changes[_]
  resource.type == "aws_s3_bucket_acl"
  acl := resource.change.after.acl
  acl == "public-read-write"
  msg := sprintf("S3 bucket ACL '%s' on resource '%s' is public and not allowed", [acl, resource.address])
}

deny[msg] {
  resource := input.resource_changes[_]
  resource.type == "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block"
  resource.change.after.block_public_acls == false
  msg := sprintf("Resource '%s' does not block public ACLs", [resource.address])
}
questions.modelAnswer: The policy has to operate against the Terraform plan's JSON representation (produced by terraform show -json on a saved plan), not the raw HCL, because the plan JSON reflects the fully resolved, final values after variables, data sources, and expressions are evaluated, which is the only reliable source of truth for what will actually be created. Each deny rule in Rego independently checks one condition across every resource_changes entry; if any rule's body evaluates to true, that rule contributes a message to the deny set, and Conftest/OPA fails the check if the deny set is non-empty, which is how multiple distinct violation types (an explicit public ACL, versus a public-access-block explicitly disabled) are each caught by their own rule rather than one overly broad check trying to catch everything. A deliberate design choice here is checking both aws_s3_bucket_acl for an explicitly public ACL and aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block for a disabled block setting, because either one alone can make a bucket effectively public, and a policy only covering one of them gives a false sense of coverage. This policy would be wired into the CI pipeline directly between terraform plan and terraform apply, failing the pipeline step if conftest test exits non-zero, which is what makes it a preventive control rather than something that generates a report after the bucket is already live.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always operate against the plan JSON, not the raw .tf files, because the plan is the fully resolved truth - all the variables and expressions have already been evaluated by the time you're looking at resource_changes, so there's no ambiguity about what's actually about to get created. Each deny rule stands on its own - if its conditions match any resource, it adds a message, and if the deny set has anything in it at all, Conftest fails the whole check. I deliberately wrote two separate rule bodies here instead of one clever combined one, because an explicitly public ACL and a public-access-block setting that's been turned off are two different ways a bucket ends up public, and I want each one caught by name so whoever sees the failure knows exactly which thing to fix. The part that actually makes this a security control and not just a nice report is where it sits in the pipeline - this runs right after plan and before apply ever gets a chance to run, so a bad bucket config fails the build instead of getting created and showing up on some dashboard three days later as something somebody now has to go clean up.
commonMistakes: Writes the policy against raw HCL instead of the resolved plan JSON
Checks only the ACL and misses the separate public-access-block setting, or vice versa
Writes one overly broad rule instead of distinct, clearly-named deny rules per violation type
Doesn't explain where in the pipeline this policy check needs to run to be preventive
keyPoints: Writes a correct, working Rego policy against plan JSON resource_changes
Checks both the ACL and the public-access-block setting as separate violation types
Correctly explains Conftest/OPA's deny-set evaluation model
Places the check between plan and apply for it to be preventive

Covers both relevant violation types (ACL and access block)
Correctly explains the deny-set evaluation model
Correctly places the check in the pipeline as a preventive gate

questions.title: Import an Existing Security Group Into Terraform State
questions.prompt: A security group was created manually in the AWS console months ago and now needs to be managed by Terraform without destroying and recreating it. Write the Terraform configuration and the command(s) needed to bring it under management safely.
questions.code:
# 1. Write the matching resource block first (best guess at current config)
resource "aws_security_group" "app_sg" {
  name        = "app-prod-sg"
  description = "Application servers - prod"
  vpc_id      = "vpc-0abc123def456789"

  ingress {
    description = "HTTPS from ALB"
    from_port   = 443
    to_port     = 443
    protocol    = "tcp"
    cidr_blocks = ["10.20.0.0/16"]
  }

  egress {
    from_port   = 0
    to_port     = 0
    protocol    = "-1"
    cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  }
}

# 2. Import the existing resource into state (Terraform >= 1.5 import block,
#    or the legacy CLI command)
import {
  to = aws_security_group.app_sg
  id = "sg-0123456789abcdef0"
}

# terraform plan   # review the diff carefully before applying
# terraform apply  # applies the import AND reconciles any config drift shown in the diff
questions.modelAnswer: The critical safety step is running terraform plan immediately after writing the import block (or the legacy terraform import command) and before ever running apply, because the plan after an import shows the diff between the resource block as written and the actual imported configuration - any attribute in the HCL that doesn't exactly match the live resource will show up as a planned change, and applying blindly risks Terraform 'fixing' the live security group to match a config block that was only a best guess at its actual rules, potentially changing or removing a rule that's currently in active use. The correct workflow is iterative: import, plan, compare the diff against the actual console configuration (or terraform show -json if preferred over reading plan output), adjust the resource block to match reality exactly, and re-plan until the diff is empty, only then applying - the apply after a clean, empty-diff plan does nothing to the live resource except update the Terraform state's bookkeeping, finally bringing the resource under real management with zero risk of unintended infrastructure change. A resource with a large or complex configuration (many rules, tags, nested blocks) often benefits from starting with a minimal resource block, importing, and then reading back the actual attributes from terraform show or the state file directly to build out the full matching configuration, rather than guessing from the console UI by hand.
questions.professionalAnswer: The step people skip, and the step that actually matters here, is running plan right after the import and reading that diff like it's trying to tell you something important - because it is. If anything in my resource block doesn't exactly match what's actually running, that shows up as a planned change, and if I apply without looking, Terraform will happily 'fix' a live security group to match my best-guess config, which might mean deleting a rule that's genuinely in use right now. So my actual workflow is: write a reasonable first pass at the resource block, import it, plan, and then treat that diff as a to-do list - go fix the config block to match reality exactly, plan again, repeat until the diff comes back completely empty. Only then do I apply, and at that point the apply isn't touching the live resource at all, it's just finalizing Terraform's bookkeeping. For anything with a lot of rules or complexity, I usually start with a bare-minimum resource block just to get it imported, then read the actual attributes straight out of the state file or terraform show instead of trying to eyeball everything correctly from the console on the first try.
commonMistakes: Runs terraform apply immediately after import without reviewing the plan diff first
Doesn't explain the risk of the live resource being modified to match a best-guess config
Doesn't describe the iterative import-plan-adjust cycle until the diff is clean
Writes the resource block from memory without verifying against actual live attributes

Insists on reviewing the plan diff before ever applying post-import
Describes the iterative adjust-and-replan cycle until the diff is empty
Explains the real risk of applying against a mismatched configuration

questions.title: Write a Prometheus Alert Rule for SLO Burn Rate
questions.prompt: Write a Prometheus alerting rule that pages when a service's error budget for a 99.9% availability SLO is burning fast enough to exhaust the 30-day budget within 2 days, using a multi-window burn rate approach.
questions.code:
groups:
  - name: slo-burn-rate-checkout-service
    rules:
      - alert: CheckoutServiceErrorBudgetBurnFast
        expr: |
          (
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout", status=~"5.."}[1h]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[1h]))
          ) > (14.4 * 0.001)
          and
          (
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[5m]))
          ) > (14.4 * 0.001)
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: page
          service: checkout
        annotations:
          summary: "Checkout service burning its 30-day error budget fast enough to exhaust it in under 2 days"
          description: "1h and 5m error rate windows both exceed a 14.4x burn rate against the 99.9% SLO."
questions.modelAnswer: The burn rate multiplier of 14.4 comes from the math of the SLO window: a 0.1% error budget (for a 99.9% SLO) burned at a constant 14.4x rate exhausts the entire 30-day budget in roughly 2 days, since 30 days / 14.4 is approximately 2.08 days - that's where the threshold in the expression comes from rather than being an arbitrary number. The reason both a long window (1h) and a short window (5m) are checked together with 'and' is to avoid two opposite failure modes: using only a long window makes the alert slow to fire (by the time an hour-long average crosses the threshold, a lot of budget may already be gone) and slow to clear after the problem resolves (the long average stays elevated well after things recover); using only a short window makes the alert noisy, firing on brief blips that don't represent a sustained, budget-threatening problem. Requiring both windows to simultaneously exceed the burn rate threshold means the alert fires quickly once a real, sustained problem starts (the short window catches it fast) while filtering out single noisy spikes (the long window confirms it's not just a 5-minute blip), which is the standard multi-window, multi-burn-rate pattern recommended for SLO-based paging. The for: 2m requirement adds a small additional debounce so a single evaluation cycle's noise doesn't immediately page, without meaningfully delaying detection of a genuine, sustained burn.
questions.professionalAnswer: The 14.4 number isn't arbitrary - it's just the math of 'how fast do you have to burn a 0.1% budget to blow through the whole 30-day allowance in about 2 days,' which works out to roughly 14.4 times your allowed baseline error rate. The reason I check both a 1-hour window and a 5-minute window together with an 'and' is to dodge two separate problems. A long window alone is slow on both ends - slow to fire because an hour-long average takes a while to cross the threshold, and slow to clear because it stays elevated for a while after things are actually fine again. A short window alone pages on every little blip that isn't really a budget-threatening trend. Requiring both to agree at once means a real, sustained problem gets caught fast through the short window, while a random five-minute spike gets filtered out because the long window never confirms it. The small 'for: 2m' on top is just there so one noisy evaluation tick doesn't immediately wake someone up - it's a tiny debounce, not a meaningful detection delay. This is the standard pattern I use anywhere I'm building SLO-based paging, not something I reinvent per service.
commonMistakes: Uses an arbitrary burn rate multiplier without connecting it to the SLO window math
Uses only a single time window, making the alert either slow or noisy
Doesn't explain why both windows must agree (the 'and' condition) rather than either one alone
Omits a for: debounce or sets it so long that detection is meaningfully delayed
keyPoints: Writes a correct multi-window burn-rate PromQL alert expression
Correctly derives and explains the burn rate multiplier from the SLO math
Explains why both a long and short window are required together
Uses an appropriate for: debounce without over-delaying detection

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct, working alerting rule
Correctly explains the burn rate multiplier derivation
Correctly explains the multi-window rationale
Appropriately uses a for: debounce

questions.title: Write an Alertmanager Routing Config for Severity-Based Escalation
questions.prompt: Write an Alertmanager configuration that routes 'page' severity alerts to PagerDuty with immediate repeat notifications, routes 'warning' severity alerts to a Slack channel with no repeat, and groups alerts by service and alertname to avoid notification storms.
questions.code:
route:
  receiver: default-slack
  group_by: ['alertname', 'service']
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h
  routes:
    - match:
        severity: page
      receiver: pagerduty-oncall
      group_wait: 10s
      repeat_interval: 15m
      continue: false
    - match:
        severity: warning
      receiver: slack-warnings
      repeat_interval: 24h
      continue: false

receivers:
  - name: default-slack
    slack_configs:
      - channel: '#alerts-general'
        send_resolved: true

  - name: pagerduty-oncall
    pagerduty_configs:
      - routing_key: '<pagerduty-integration-key>'
        send_resolved: true

  - name: slack-warnings
    slack_configs:
      - channel: '#alerts-warnings'
        send_resolved: true
questions.modelAnswer: group_by: ['alertname', 'service'] is what prevents a notification storm during a real incident: without it, Alertmanager's default grouping could fire a separate notification per unique label combination, meaning a single root cause affecting one service could generate dozens of near-identical pages for every pod or instance label variation, while grouping by alertname and service bundles all of those into one notification per actual incident, which is both less noisy and gives the responder the full scope of what's affected in one place rather than piecing it together from a flood of separate alerts. The severity-based routing tree uses continue: false on each matched route so a 'page' severity alert is handled only by the PagerDuty route and doesn't also fall through to the default Slack receiver, avoiding duplicate notifications for the same alert through two channels. The repeat_interval difference is deliberate: page-severity alerts repeat every 15 minutes specifically so an unacknowledged, still-firing critical alert keeps escalating rather than notifying once and going silent if the first page is missed, while warning-severity alerts repeat only every 24 hours, reflecting that they're informational enough not to warrant repeated interruption. group_wait: 10s on the page route (shorter than the default group_wait) ensures a genuinely critical alert doesn't sit waiting to be grouped with other alerts for the default 30 seconds before the first notification goes out.
questions.professionalAnswer: The group_by on alertname and service is the single most important line in here for anyone who's ever been paged 40 times for the same actual problem - without it, a bad deploy touching one service can spray a separate alert per instance or pod label, and grouping collapses all of that into one notification that actually tells you the scope of what's wrong instead of burying you in duplicates. I use continue: false on both the page and warning routes specifically so a page-severity alert only goes to PagerDuty and doesn't also leak into the general Slack channel as a second, redundant notification - that kind of double-notification is exactly the thing that trains people to tune out alerts. The repeat_interval split is intentional too - page alerts repeat every 15 minutes because if the first page gets missed or snoozed, I want it to keep escalating, not fire once and go quiet for hours. Warnings repeat once a day at most, because they're not something I want waking anyone up repeatedly. And I shorten group_wait specifically on the page route - the default 30-second wait to let alerts group together is fine for Slack warnings, but for something page-worthy I want that first notification out in 10 seconds, not waiting around for company.
commonMistakes: Omits group_by entirely, risking notification storms during real incidents
Doesn't use continue: false, causing duplicate notifications across multiple receivers
Uses the same repeat_interval for page and warning severities
Doesn't shorten group_wait for the critical/page route
keyPoints: Writes a correct Alertmanager routing tree with severity-based receivers
Correctly uses group_by to prevent notification storms
Correctly uses continue: false to avoid duplicate cross-receiver notifications
Differentiates repeat_interval and group_wait appropriately by severity

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct, working Alertmanager configuration
Correctly explains group_by's role in preventing notification storms
Correctly explains continue: false and routing isolation
Appropriately differentiates timing by severity

questions.title: Configure an OpenTelemetry Collector to Export Traces to a Tracing Backend
questions.prompt: Write an OpenTelemetry Collector configuration that receives traces via OTLP, batches them, adds a resource attribute for the deployment environment, and exports them to a tracing backend, with a separate pipeline sampling only 20% of traces for cost control.
questions.code:
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318

processors:
  batch:
    timeout: 5s
    send_batch_size: 1024

  resource:
    attributes:
      - key: deployment.environment
        value: "production"
        action: upsert

  probabilistic_sampler:
    sampling_percentage: 20

exporters:
  otlp/tracing-backend:
    endpoint: "tracing-backend.internal:4317"
    tls:
      insecure: false

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [resource, probabilistic_sampler, batch]
      exporters: [otlp/tracing-backend]
questions.modelAnswer: The receiver accepts OTLP over both gRPC (port 4317, generally preferred for lower overhead) and HTTP (port 4318, useful for clients or environments where gRPC is awkward), giving instrumented applications flexibility in how they ship spans to the collector regardless of their runtime's gRPC support. The processor order in the pipeline matters: resource attribution happens before sampling so every span, including ones that will be dropped, is correctly tagged for the brief period it exists in the pipeline (useful for any pre-sampling metrics derived from the stream), and batching happens last specifically so the collector batches only the spans that survived sampling, which is what actually delivers the cost reduction - batching before sampling would still batch and prepare for export spans that are about to be discarded anyway, wasting the work. The probabilistic_sampler at 20% is head-based sampling applied at the collector rather than in the application, meaning the sampling decision is centralized and can be changed without redeploying every instrumented service, though it comes with a tradeoff worth naming: at 20% sampling, a rare but important trace (an error that occurs in only 1% of requests) has a reduced but non-zero chance of being captured, so teams needing guaranteed capture of error traces specifically would pair this with tail-based sampling or an explicit always-sample-on-error rule rather than relying on uniform probabilistic sampling alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: I accept OTLP over both gRPC and HTTP because not every client or environment plays nicely with gRPC, and giving both options means I'm not fighting some legacy service's networking setup just to get traces out of it. The order of processors here is deliberate, not arbitrary - resource tagging happens before sampling so every span gets correctly labeled while it's still in the pipeline, and batching happens dead last so I'm only batching and shipping the 20% of spans that actually survived sampling, instead of doing all that batching work on spans about to get thrown away anyway. Doing sampling at the collector instead of in each application's SDK is the part I actually care about operationally - it means I can change the sampling rate centrally without redeploying 40 services. The honest caveat I always give teams on probabilistic sampling at 20%: if something fails in only 1% of requests, there's a real chance that failure's trace just doesn't get captured. If error visibility specifically matters more than general cost control, I pair this with tail-based sampling or an explicit rule that always keeps error traces regardless of the sampling percentage, rather than trusting uniform random sampling to catch the rare important thing.
commonMistakes: Orders processors incorrectly, batching before sampling and wasting work on discarded spans
Doesn't explain the tradeoff of probabilistic sampling missing rare but important traces
Omits resource attribution or applies it after sampling
Doesn't explain the benefit of centralizing sampling decisions at the collector versus the SDK

Correctly orders processors (resource tagging before sampling, batching last)
Explains the cost/coverage tradeoff of probabilistic sampling
Explains the benefit of centralizing sampling at the collector

questions.title: Write a HorizontalPodAutoscaler and Confirm Cluster Autoscaler Compatibility
questions.prompt: Write a Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler manifest that scales a deployment between 3 and 20 replicas based on 70% average CPU utilization, and explain the one node-level setting you'd verify exists before trusting this HPA to actually relieve load under a real traffic spike.
questions.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: checkout-api-hpa
  namespace: production
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: checkout-api
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 30
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
questions.modelAnswer: The one thing I'd verify before trusting this HPA under a real spike is that a Cluster Autoscaler (or equivalent managed node autoscaling, such as AKS's or EKS's cluster autoscaling add-on) is actually enabled and configured on the node pool backing this namespace, with a maxNodes ceiling high enough to actually accommodate 20 replicas' worth of resource requests. The HPA scaling replicas from 3 to 20 is meaningless if the underlying nodes don't have room to schedule the extra 17 pods - without Cluster Autoscaler, those new replicas would sit Pending while already-provisioned nodes stay full, and the HPA would appear to be 'working' (replica count going up in the dashboard) while delivering zero actual relief to the overloaded service. The scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds of 300 (5 minutes) versus scaleUp's 30 seconds is also a deliberate asymmetry: scaling up fast is low-risk (extra capacity just costs money briefly) while scaling down fast is higher-risk (prematurely removing capacity right as a traffic spike subsides briefly, then having to scale back up again, causing user-visible thrashing), so the longer stabilization window on scale-down avoids reacting to a brief dip in load as if it were a sustained one.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I'd trust this HPA to actually do anything under a real spike, I'm checking that Cluster Autoscaler, or whatever the managed equivalent is on AKS or EKS, is actually turned on for the node pool underneath this, with a node ceiling that can genuinely fit 20 replicas' worth of CPU and memory requests. An HPA cranking replicas from 3 to 20 means nothing if there's no room on the nodes for the other 17 pods - they just sit there Pending while the dashboard shows the replica count climbing and nobody's actual problem gets solved. I also set scaleUp and scaleDown stabilization windows asymmetrically on purpose - scaling up fast is basically free risk, worst case you spend a little extra money for a few minutes. Scaling down fast is the one that bites you, because if load dips for twenty seconds and you immediately rip away capacity, then load comes right back and you're scaling up again, which is exactly the flapping behavior that makes autoscaling look unreliable to everyone watching it. A five-minute scale-down window versus a thirty-second scale-up window is a deliberate bias toward stability over cost-optimization in the one direction where getting it wrong is actually painful.
commonMistakes: Writes the HPA manifest without checking for Cluster Autoscaler / node capacity at all
Doesn't explain the Pending-pod failure mode when node capacity is insufficient
Uses symmetric scale-up/scale-down stabilization windows without justification
Doesn't connect maxReplicas to an actual node pool ceiling
keyPoints: Writes a correct HPA manifest with appropriate scaling behavior settings
Identifies Cluster Autoscaler / node capacity as the critical dependency to verify
Explains the Pending-pod failure mode when node capacity is missing

questions.title: Write a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy Restricting Cross-Namespace Traffic
questions.prompt: Write a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy for the 'payments' namespace that denies all ingress traffic by default, then explicitly allows ingress only from pods labeled app=checkout-api in the 'storefront' namespace, on port 8443.
questions.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: payments
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-checkout-api-ingress
  namespace: payments
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: storefront
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: checkout-api
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8443
questions.modelAnswer: Two separate NetworkPolicy objects are needed because of how Kubernetes NetworkPolicy semantics work: an empty podSelector: {} with no ingress rules and policyTypes: [Ingress] matches every pod in the namespace and denies all ingress to them by default, establishing the deny-by-default posture, and a second policy then explicitly allows the one path that should work - this combination is necessary because NetworkPolicies are additive (multiple policies selecting the same pod are combined with OR, not AND), so a single policy can't both deny everything and then carve out an exception in one object the way a sequential firewall ruleset might. The ingress rule's 'from' combines a namespaceSelector and a podSelector within the same 'from' entry, which is deliberately an AND condition - traffic is only allowed if it originates from a pod matching app=checkout-api AND that pod is in a namespace matching the storefront label, which is more restrictive and correct than listing them as two separate array entries under 'from', since two separate entries would be evaluated as OR (any pod in storefront OR any pod labeled checkout-api anywhere), incorrectly widening access. The namespaceSelector uses the built-in kubernetes.io/metadata.name label (automatically present on every namespace since Kubernetes 1.21) rather than assuming a custom label exists, which makes the policy portable without relying on the storefront namespace having been manually labeled first.
questions.professionalAnswer: This needs two separate policy objects because of how NetworkPolicy actually combines rules - they're additive, OR'd together, not like a sequential firewall where rule order and explicit deny-then-allow logic works in one list. So the first policy is pure deny-by-default: empty pod selector, no ingress rules, which locks down every pod in the namespace. The second policy then carves out the one exception. The detail that trips people up constantly is putting the namespaceSelector and podSelector in the same 'from' entry versus two separate entries - same entry means AND, it has to be a checkout-api pod AND it has to be in the storefront namespace. Split them into two separate list entries and it silently becomes OR - any pod in storefront at all, or any checkout-api-labeled pod from any namespace - which is a much bigger hole than anyone intended and the kind of mistake that doesn't show up until someone actually tests from an unexpected pod. I use the built-in kubernetes.io/metadata.name label for the namespace match specifically because it's there automatically on every namespace since 1.21 - I don't want this policy silently failing to match anything because somebody forgot to manually label the storefront namespace with a custom key.
commonMistakes: Writes only the allow rule without a separate default-deny policy, leaving other ingress paths open
Puts namespaceSelector and podSelector in separate 'from' array entries, accidentally widening access to OR instead of AND
Uses a custom namespace label instead of the built-in kubernetes.io/metadata.name, risking an unlabeled namespace silently failing to match
Doesn't specify policyTypes, leaving the policy's intended scope ambiguous
keyPoints: Writes both a default-deny policy and a correctly scoped allow policy
Correctly combines namespaceSelector and podSelector within one 'from' entry for AND semantics
Uses the built-in namespace label for portability
Explains the additive (OR) nature of multiple NetworkPolicy objects

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes correct default-deny and allow NetworkPolicy manifests
Correctly combines selectors for AND semantics within 'from'
Correctly explains NetworkPolicy's additive/OR combination rules
Uses portable, built-in namespace labeling

questions.title: Write a Least-Privilege RBAC Role and Workload Identity Binding
questions.prompt: Write a Kubernetes Role and RoleBinding granting a service account named 'deploy-bot' in the 'ci' namespace only the ability to get, list, and patch Deployments in the 'production' namespace, nothing else.
questions.code:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: deployment-patcher
  namespace: production
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "patch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: deploy-bot-can-patch-deployments
  namespace: production
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: deploy-bot
    namespace: ci
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  name: deployment-patcher
questions.modelAnswer: The Role is namespaced to 'production' (not a ClusterRole) because the requirement is scoped to one namespace, and using a Role rather than a ClusterRole means this service account's permissions can never be interpreted as applying cluster-wide even if someone later copies this pattern carelessly elsewhere - a Role is structurally confined to the namespace it's defined in. The apiGroups: ['apps'] is required specifically because Deployments live in the apps API group, not the core (empty string) group; a common mistake is omitting this or using the wrong group, which causes the rule to silently not match the resource it was intended for, and kubectl auth can-i checks would then correctly report no permission despite the Role looking superficially correct. The RoleBinding subject references the service account by name and, critically, by its own namespace ('ci'), separate from the RoleBinding's own namespace ('production') - this is exactly how Kubernetes allows a service account from one namespace to be granted permissions in a different namespace, and getting either namespace field wrong (binding to a service account that doesn't exist in the referenced namespace) fails silently rather than erroring, so verifying with kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deploy-bot patch deployments -n production after applying is the correct way to confirm the binding actually works as intended rather than trusting the YAML alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: I use a namespaced Role here, not a ClusterRole, specifically because the ask is scoped to one namespace - a Role can't accidentally apply cluster-wide even if someone copies this YAML somewhere else later without thinking about it, which a ClusterRole absolutely could. The apiGroups field is the one thing I double check every time, because Deployments are in 'apps', not the core group, and getting that wrong doesn't throw an error - the rule just silently doesn't match anything, and you'd have a Role that looks completely reasonable but grants nothing. The RoleBinding's subject has its own namespace field, 'ci', which is separate from the RoleBinding's own namespace, 'production' - that cross-namespace reference is exactly the mechanism that lets a service account that lives in one namespace get granted access in a totally different one. I never trust that this is wired correctly just from reading the YAML, though - I always run kubectl auth can-i as that exact service account against the exact verb and resource I intended, because a typo in either namespace field fails silently instead of erroring, and that's not something you want to discover for the first time when a CI pipeline unexpectedly can't deploy.

Omits or gets the apiGroups value wrong for Deployments
Confuses the service account's own namespace with the RoleBinding's namespace
Doesn't verify the binding with kubectl auth can-i after applying

Correctly specifies the apps API group for Deployments
Correctly cross-references the service account's own namespace in the RoleBinding subject
Proposes verifying the binding with kubectl auth can-i rather than trusting the YAML alone

Correctly handles the apiGroups for Deployments
Correctly handles cross-namespace service account reference
Proposes a concrete verification step

questions.title: Add a Container Image Scan Gate to a GitHub Actions Workflow
questions.prompt: Write a GitHub Actions job that builds a Docker image, scans it with Trivy, and fails the workflow only on critical or high severity vulnerabilities that have an available fix.
questions.code:
jobs:
  build-and-scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t myorg/checkout-api:${{ github.sha }} .

      - name: Scan image with Trivy
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.28.0
        with:
          image-ref: myorg/checkout-api:${{ github.sha }}
          severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'
          ignore-unfixed: true
          exit-code: '1'
          format: 'sarif'
          output: 'trivy-results.sarif'

      - name: Upload Trivy scan results
        if: always()
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        with:
          sarif_file: 'trivy-results.sarif'
questions.modelAnswer: The combination of severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH' with ignore-unfixed: true and exit-code: '1' is what implements the intended policy precisely: severity restricts findings under consideration to only critical and high, ignore-unfixed drops any finding that has no available patched version from consideration entirely (since blocking a build on an unfixable finding only trains teams to bypass the scanner), and exit-code: '1' is what actually causes Trivy to exit non-zero and fail the GitHub Actions step when any finding survives both filters - without an explicit exit-code set, some scanner actions default to reporting without failing the build, which would silently turn this from a gate into a report. The if: always() on the upload step ensures scan results are still uploaded to the Security tab even when the scan step itself fails the build, which matters because a failed build is exactly the moment someone most needs to see the specific findings, not only the passing-build case. Using the image tagged with github.sha rather than a generic 'latest' tag ensures the exact image that was just built is the one being scanned, avoiding any ambiguity about which build the scan results actually correspond to, which matters once more than one workflow run might be building images concurrently.
questions.professionalAnswer: The policy this implements is deliberately narrow: critical or high, with a fix available, full stop, fails the build - and all three of those pieces matter together. severity filters down to critical and high only, ignore-unfixed drops anything with no patch available yet because blocking on something nobody can fix just trains people to disable the scanner, and exit-code is the thing that actually makes any of this matter - without setting it explicitly, plenty of scan actions will happily report findings and still exit zero, which means the build 'passes' and nobody downstream even knows there's a problem. I always upload the SARIF results with if: always(), specifically so that when the build does fail, whoever's looking at it can see exactly which CVEs tripped it in the Security tab, not just a generic 'Trivy step failed' in the logs. And I tag the image with the commit SHA instead of something generic like 'latest' before scanning it, because the second two workflow runs are building around the same time, a generic tag makes it genuinely ambiguous which build's results you're actually looking at.
commonMistakes: Omits ignore-unfixed, blocking builds on vulnerabilities with no available fix
Doesn't explicitly set exit-code, silently turning the scan into a report rather than a gate
Doesn't upload scan results on failure, hiding the specific findings from whoever sees the failed build
Scans a generic 'latest' tag instead of the exact image just built
keyPoints: Writes a correct Trivy scanning step with severity and fixability filters
Explicitly sets exit-code so the scan actually gates the build
Uploads results even on failure for visibility into specific findings
Scans the exact image just built, tagged unambiguously

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct, working build-and-scan workflow
Correctly filters by severity and fixability
Ensures the scan actually gates the build via exit-code
Uploads results on failure for visibility

questions.title: Generate and Attach an SBOM in a CI Pipeline
questions.prompt: Write a GitHub Actions step that generates a CycloneDX SBOM for a built container image using Syft, and attaches it as a build artifact alongside the image.
questions.code:
jobs:
  build-and-sbom:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t myorg/checkout-api:${{ github.sha }} .

      - name: Install Syft
        uses: anchore/sbom-action/download-syft@v0.17.2

      - name: Generate SBOM (CycloneDX JSON)
        run: |
          syft myorg/checkout-api:${{ github.sha }} \
            -o cyclonedx-json=sbom-checkout-api-${{ github.sha }}.json

      - name: Upload SBOM artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: sbom-checkout-api-${{ github.sha }}
          path: sbom-checkout-api-${{ github.sha }}.json
          retention-days: 400
questions.modelAnswer: Generating the SBOM against the exact image built in this run, tagged with github.sha, rather than pulling some tag like 'latest' from a registry, guarantees the SBOM accurately reflects what's actually in this specific artifact rather than possibly describing a different build that happened to share a tag - an SBOM that doesn't correspond exactly to the image it claims to describe is worse than no SBOM, because it's actively misleading during an incident. Choosing CycloneDX JSON as the output format is a deliberate interoperability decision: CycloneDX (alongside SPDX) is one of the two dominant standard formats most downstream vulnerability-matching and compliance tooling expects, so emitting it in a non-standard or tool-proprietary format would require custom tooling everywhere it's consumed. The retention-days: 400 on the artifact upload is set deliberately long rather than left at GitHub's shorter default, because the entire operational value of an SBOM is being able to look up what was in an artifact that's still running in production potentially a year later when a new CVE is disclosed - an SBOM that's already expired and deleted by the time it's actually needed provides no value at all, so retention has to be tied to realistic production artifact lifetimes, not CI's default assumption that build artifacts are short-lived debugging aids.
questions.professionalAnswer: I generate the SBOM against the exact tag that was just built in this run, never against something like 'latest', because an SBOM that doesn't precisely correspond to the artifact it's describing is actively worse than having none - it gives someone false confidence about what's actually in the image they're worried about. CycloneDX JSON specifically because that's one of the two formats, alongside SPDX, that basically everything downstream expects - vulnerability matching tools, compliance tooling - so there's no reason to emit something proprietary that nobody else can consume without custom glue code. The thing I always have to correct people on is artifact retention - GitHub's default retention on build artifacts is short, because most CI artifacts are debugging aids nobody needs in six months. An SBOM is the opposite case entirely - its whole point is being queryable a year from now when some library gets a CVE disclosed and someone needs to know instantly whether this exact image, which might still be running in production, is affected. If the SBOM already expired and got deleted by then, you built it for nothing.
commonMistakes: Generates the SBOM against a generic tag instead of the exact image built in this run
Uses a non-standard or proprietary output format instead of CycloneDX or SPDX
Leaves artifact retention at CI's short default, causing the SBOM to expire before it's needed
Doesn't tie the SBOM's filename/identity to the specific build it describes

Uses a standard, interoperable format (CycloneDX or SPDX)
Sets a retention period matching realistic production artifact lifetimes
Correctly ties the SBOM identity to the specific build/commit

Uses a standard format appropriately
Ensures SBOM corresponds exactly to the built artifact
Sets appropriate long-term retention

questions.title: Write an Argo CD Application Manifest for GitOps Deployment
questions.prompt: Write an Argo CD Application manifest that syncs a Helm chart from a Git repository into the 'production' namespace, automatically syncing on changes but requiring self-healing and pruning to be explicitly enabled.
questions.code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme-corp/checkout-api-chart.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: charts/checkout-api
    helm:
      valueFiles:
        - values-production.yaml
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: production
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=false
    retry:
      limit: 3
      backoff:
        duration: 10s
        factor: 2
        maxDuration: 3m
questions.modelAnswer: The three sync-related flags each guard against a distinct failure mode, and the task's framing of 'requiring them to be explicitly enabled' matters because none of these default to on. prune: true means resources removed from the Git source get deleted from the cluster automatically; without it, deleting a resource from the Helm chart leaves an orphaned resource running in the cluster indefinitely, silently diverging from what Git describes. selfHeal: true means a manual kubectl edit made directly against a resource Argo CD manages gets automatically reverted back to match Git on the next sync, which is the mechanism that actually enforces Git as the single source of truth - without it, someone's emergency console fix during an incident would persist indefinitely until the next unrelated deploy happened to overwrite it, which is an unpredictable and unintentional way to revert a manual change. The retry block with exponential backoff (10s, doubling, capped at 3m) handles transient sync failures (a brief API server hiccup) without endlessly hammering the cluster API on every retry attempt. CreateNamespace=false is a deliberate choice here, not an oversight, requiring the production namespace to already exist and be managed through its own deliberate process rather than letting a Helm chart sync implicitly create a production namespace as a side effect, which is a reasonable guardrail against an application's chart accidentally creating infrastructure-level resources.
questions.professionalAnswer: Each of these three flags is guarding against something specific, and none of them are on by default, which is exactly why the ask here is to turn them on explicitly rather than assume they're already there. prune means if someone removes a resource from the chart, Argo CD actually deletes it from the cluster - without that, you get orphaned resources quietly running that Git no longer even mentions. selfHeal is the one I consider non-negotiable for true GitOps - it means if someone does a manual kubectl edit directly against something Argo manages, that edit gets reverted back to match Git on the very next sync. Without selfHeal, a 2am emergency console fix just sits there indefinitely, as a silent, undocumented exception to what Git says should be running, until some unrelated future deploy happens to stomp on it by accident. I keep CreateNamespace set to false here deliberately - I don't want an application-level Helm chart able to implicitly create a production namespace as a side effect of a sync; namespace creation is its own deliberate decision, not something that should ride along with a chart deploy. The retry block with backoff is just there so a brief API hiccup doesn't turn into the sync hammering the cluster repeatedly - it backs off and gives up gracefully after a reasonable number of tries.
commonMistakes: Omits prune or selfHeal, leaving the cluster able to drift from Git silently
Doesn't explain that selfHeal is what actually enforces Git as the source of truth against manual changes
Enables CreateNamespace without considering whether namespace creation should be a separate, deliberate process
Omits retry/backoff handling for transient sync failures

Correctly explains prune's role in preventing orphaned resources
Correctly explains selfHeal's role in reverting manual drift
Makes a deliberate, justified choice about namespace creation

questions.title: Write a Canary Deployment Stage With an Automated Rollback Gate
questions.prompt: Write a CI/CD pipeline stage (in GitHub Actions-style YAML, calling kubectl/Argo Rollouts conceptually) that shifts 10% of traffic to a new version, waits, checks an error-rate metric, and automatically rolls back if the error rate exceeds a threshold.
questions.code:
jobs:
  canary-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Deploy canary (10% traffic)
        run: |
          kubectl argo rollouts set image checkout-api \
            checkout-api=myorg/checkout-api:${{ github.sha }} -n production
          kubectl argo rollouts status checkout-api -n production --timeout 60s

      - name: Wait for canary bake time
        run: sleep 300  # 5 minutes of real traffic against the 10% canary step

      - name: Check canary error rate against SLO threshold
        id: check
        run: |
          ERROR_RATE=$(curl -s "https://prometheus.internal/api/v1/query" \
            --data-urlencode 'query=sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout-api",version="canary",status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout-api",version="canary"}[5m]))' \
            | jq -r '.data.result[0].value[1]')
          echo "canary_error_rate=$ERROR_RATE" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          awk -v rate="$ERROR_RATE" 'BEGIN { exit !(rate > 0.02) }'

      - name: Promote canary to full rollout
        if: success()
        run: kubectl argo rollouts promote checkout-api -n production

      - name: Automated rollback on breached threshold
        if: failure()
        run: kubectl argo rollouts abort checkout-api -n production
questions.modelAnswer: The structural pattern here is that the error-rate check step's own exit code is what the pipeline's conditional logic hinges on: the awk command deliberately inverts the comparison (exit !(rate > 0.02)) so that the step exits non-zero, and therefore 'fails' in GitHub Actions terms, precisely when the error rate exceeds the 2% threshold, which is what makes if: failure() on the rollback step and if: success() on the promote step work as a correct, automatic either-or branch rather than needing manual judgment. The bake time (a fixed wait, here 5 minutes) is deliberately before the check, not instead of it, because a canary needs to accumulate enough real traffic and real time for the error-rate query's own window (the PromQL query's [5m] range) to reflect genuine canary behavior rather than a near-empty, statistically meaningless sample from the first few seconds after the traffic shift. Querying specifically on version="canary" rather than the service's overall error rate is what isolates the canary's own behavior from the stable version still serving 90% of traffic - without that label filter, a canary with a severe bug could be fully diluted by the healthy 90% and never trip the threshold at all, defeating the entire purpose of a canary check. The rollback action (argo rollouts abort) needs to be a fast, automatic, no-human-in-the-loop action specifically because the entire value of an automated canary gate is catching and reverting a bad release before it reaches more users, not generating an alert for a human to act on minutes later after more damage is already done.
questions.professionalAnswer: The trick that makes this whole thing work automatically instead of needing someone watching a dashboard is that inverted exit code in the check step - it deliberately fails the step when the error rate crosses 2%, and GitHub Actions' if: success() and if: failure() branch cleanly off of that single signal, no human judgment required in the moment. I always put a real bake time before the check, not instead of it, because checking error rate three seconds after shifting traffic is checking basically nothing - the PromQL window itself needs real traffic flowing through the canary for the number to mean anything. The detail that actually makes this a canary check and not just a general health check is filtering specifically on version="canary" - if I query the service's overall error rate instead, a badly broken canary serving only 10% of traffic gets diluted by the healthy 90% still on the old version, and the threshold never trips even though the new version is genuinely broken. And the rollback itself has to be instant and automatic, no pause for a human to notice and act - the entire point of wiring this up this way is catching a bad release and pulling it back before it does real damage to more users, not generating a ticket for someone to look at after the fact.
commonMistakes: Doesn't tie the pipeline's conditional branching to the check step's own exit code
Checks error rate immediately with no bake time, getting a statistically meaningless sample
Queries overall service error rate instead of filtering specifically on the canary version
Makes rollback a manual or delayed action instead of immediate and automatic
keyPoints: Writes a correct canary stage with a working automated rollback/promote branch
Includes a real bake time before evaluating the error rate
Correctly isolates the canary version's own error rate from the stable version
Explains why rollback must be immediate and automatic, not human-gated

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct, working canary pipeline stage
Includes an appropriate bake time before evaluation
Correctly isolates canary-specific metrics

questions.title: Write a Cost Allocation Tagging Policy and a Cost Explorer CLI Query by Team
questions.prompt: Design and write an AWS Organizations tag policy enforcing a mandatory 'team' and 'cost-center' tag on all taggable data platform resources, plus the Cost Explorer CLI call you'd run monthly to break down spend by team for a chargeback report.
questions.modelAnswer: The Organizations tag policy operates as a compliance/visibility layer, not a hard preventive control by itself -- enforced_for flags resources as non-compliant in the Tag Policies compliance report if the tag is missing or has a value outside the allowed list, but a tag policy alone does not block resource creation; to actually prevent untagged resources from being created, this needs to be paired with an SCP (denying resource creation actions unless the required tag is present in the request, using aws:RequestTag conditions) or a Service Catalog / Config-rule-based preventive control. I'd deploy the tag policy first for visibility and a compliance dashboard, and add the SCP enforcement as the actual blocking mechanism once teams have had a grace period to retrofit existing resources, since a sudden hard block on an environment with lots of pre-existing untagged resources tends to cause more operational pain than it prevents. For the Cost Explorer query, --group-by Type=TAG,Key=team requires that 'team' first be activated as a cost allocation tag in the Billing console (tag policies and cost allocation tag activation are two separate, both-required steps) -- a tag can be enforced by policy and still invisible to Cost Explorer if it was never activated for cost allocation, which is a common gap that makes a chargeback report quietly incomplete for weeks before anyone notices.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be upfront that a tag policy alone doesn't stop anyone from creating an untagged resource -- it just makes that resource show up as non-compliant in a report. If the real goal is actually preventing untagged resources, that needs an SCP with a RequestTag condition denying the create action outright, and I'd roll that out as a second phase after giving teams time to tag what already exists, rather than flipping on a hard block immediately and breaking everyone's existing automation. For the Cost Explorer side, there's a step people forget constantly: the tag has to be separately activated as a cost allocation tag in Billing before Cost Explorer's group-by will even see it -- having a tag policy enforcing 'team' doesn't automatically make 'team' usable in a cost report. I'd check that activation explicitly before telling finance the chargeback report is ready, because otherwise you get a clean-looking tag policy and a cost report that's quietly missing data for weeks.

Doesn't mention the separate requirement to activate a tag as a cost allocation tag in Billing before Cost Explorer can group by it
Rolls out a hard SCP-based tagging block with no grace period for existing untagged resources
Scopes the tag policy to too few or the wrong resource types for the platform's actual services

Writes a correct Cost Explorer CLI query grouped by the tag

questions.title: Write an SCP Denying Non-Approved Regions for a Data Platform Organization
questions.prompt: Compliance requires that no data platform resources are ever created outside us-east-1 and eu-west-1, across every member account in the organization, with an explicit exception for global/non-regional services like IAM and CloudFront. Write the Service Control Policy.
questions.modelAnswer: The structural key to this SCP is using NotAction together with a region Condition rather than trying to Deny every regional service action individually -- NotAction here means the Deny statement applies to every action EXCEPT the ones listed (IAM, Organizations, CloudFront, Route 53, Support, STS, Budgets, Cost Explorer -- all genuinely global or non-regional services), which is both far more maintainable than enumerating every regional AWS service explicitly and correctly future-proofs against new services, since any new regional service AWS launches is automatically covered by this deny without the policy needing an update. The Condition using aws:RequestedRegion with StringNotEquals against the two approved regions means the deny only fires when a request targets a region outside the approved list, so creating an S3 bucket or Redshift cluster in us-east-1 or eu-west-1 is unaffected, while the same call targeting ap-southeast-1 is blocked at the IAM evaluation level before it ever reaches the service. I'd explicitly include sts:*, budgets:*, and ce:* in the exception list because those are genuinely non-regional or need to function platform-wide regardless of region restrictions (STS for assume-role chains across the org, Budgets/Cost Explorer for the finance visibility this very platform needs); omitting them is a common mistake that breaks unrelated functionality while trying to lock down regions. I'd test this against a non-production OU first with a deliberate attempt to create a resource in a disallowed region, confirming it's denied, before attaching it broadly, since an SCP mistake applies org-wide immediately and is a very blunt instrument to get wrong.
questions.professionalAnswer: The pattern I'd use is NotAction plus a region condition, not a long Deny list of every regional action I can think of -- NotAction flips it around to 'deny everything except this short list of truly global services,' which means any new regional AWS service automatically gets caught by this policy without me having to remember to update it later. The condition is aws:RequestedRegion not equal to our two approved regions, so anything targeting us-east-1 or eu-west-1 sails through untouched, and anything else gets denied before it even reaches the service. I'd be careful about the exception list -- IAM and CloudFront are the obvious ones, but I'd also exclude STS, Budgets, and Cost Explorer explicitly, because those need to work regardless of region and I've seen SCPs like this accidentally break assume-role chains or cost visibility because someone forgot them. Before attaching this broadly, I'd test it against one non-production OU first and actually try to create something in a disallowed region to confirm it gets denied, because an SCP mistake here is organization-wide and immediate.

questions.title: A Terraform State Lock Is Stuck After a CI Runner Crashed
questions.prompt: A CI pipeline running terraform apply was forcibly killed mid-run when the runner crashed. Now every subsequent plan or apply fails immediately with a state lock error, but no one is actually running Terraform. Walk through how you'd diagnose and safely resolve this.
questions.modelAnswer: The lock error itself tells you the lock record still exists in the backend (a DynamoDB item, an azurerm blob lease, or equivalent) even though the process that created it is gone, since Terraform's lock is advisory and tied to a process that's supposed to release it on exit, which a crashed runner never got the chance to do. The first diagnostic step is confirming nothing is actually still running - checking the CI system for any lingering or zombie job, and checking with the team for any human running Terraform locally against the same state right now - because force-unlocking while something genuinely is still applying is exactly the scenario the lock exists to prevent, and doing it anyway risks real state corruption from a concurrent write. Once genuine abandonment is confirmed, terraform force-unlock <lock-id> removes the stale lock, using the lock ID reported in the original error message. The step that actually matters most, though, happens after unlocking: running terraform plan immediately to check whether the crashed apply left the state in a partially-applied condition - some resources created, others not, matching neither the old nor the fully-intended new configuration - since a mid-apply crash can leave real infrastructure in an inconsistent state that the plan will surface as unexpected changes, and those need to be reviewed carefully rather than blindly applied, in case the crash happened partway through a resource that's now in a transitional, possibly broken state in the cloud itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: The lock error means exactly what it says - there's still a lock record sitting in the backend from that crashed run, because Terraform's lock is cooperative, the process is supposed to clean it up on exit, and a crash means that cleanup never happened. Before I touch anything, I check two things: is there actually a zombie job still running somewhere in CI, and is anyone on the team running Terraform locally against this same state right now. Force-unlocking while something's genuinely still in flight is the one way to make this situation actually dangerous instead of just annoying. Once I'm sure it's genuinely abandoned, terraform force-unlock with the lock ID from the error clears it. But the real work starts after that - I immediately run a plan, not an apply, because a crash mid-apply can leave infrastructure in a half-done state, some resources created, some not, and the plan is going to show me a diff that might not match what I expect at all. I read that diff carefully before doing anything else, because applying blindly on top of a state that might reflect a partially-created resource is how one crashed CI job turns into two separate incidents instead of one.

Doesn't check for a partially-applied state after unlocking
Runs terraform apply immediately after unlocking instead of reviewing a plan first
Doesn't look up the specific lock ID from the error before force-unlocking

Confirms no process is genuinely still running before force-unlocking
Uses terraform force-unlock with the correct lock ID
Reviews a plan for partially-applied state before any further apply

questions.title: Terraform Plan Keeps Showing the Same Drift Every Run
questions.prompt: Every single terraform plan against a particular resource shows the same unwanted change, even immediately after running apply to 'fix' it. The resource appears correct when you check the cloud console. Walk through what's actually happening and how you'd resolve it.
questions.modelAnswer: A change that reappears identically after every apply, with the console showing the resource as correct, is the signature of a provider-side normalization mismatch rather than real infrastructure drift - some attribute is being returned by the cloud API in a form (different casing, a reordered list, a default value the API injects that isn't present in the configuration) that doesn't byte-for-byte match what's written in the HCL, so Terraform's diff logic considers it changed even though functionally nothing is different. The diagnostic step is running terraform plan with detailed exit codes or inspecting the specific attribute flagged in the diff closely - often it's something like a JSON policy document where the API returns keys in a different order, or a list attribute where the API silently reorders entries, or a default tag/attribute the provider injects that was never declared in the configuration at all. Depending on the specific cause, the fix is either normalizing the configuration to match what the API actually returns (using jsonencode consistently and comparing against the exact returned structure for a JSON policy mismatch), using ignore_changes in a lifecycle block for an attribute that's genuinely managed outside Terraform and legitimately expected to differ, or in a true provider bug, pinning to a known-good provider version and filing or searching for the issue upstream, since this specific symptom pattern is a well-known class of provider bugs that gets fixed over time across provider releases.
questions.professionalAnswer: When the same diff shows up every single time, right after an apply that should have fixed it, and the console looks completely fine, that's not real drift - that's a normalization mismatch between what the config says and what the API hands back. Something about the attribute's format doesn't match byte for byte, even though functionally it's identical - classic culprits are a JSON policy document where key order differs, or a list the API quietly reorders, or some default value the provider injects that was never in my config to begin with. My first move is looking closely at exactly what the diff claims is changing, not just that something is changing. If it's a JSON structure issue, I make sure I'm using jsonencode consistently and actually compare it against what the API returns. If it's something genuinely managed outside Terraform that's supposed to differ, lifecycle ignore_changes is the right tool, not a workaround - I'm telling Terraform explicitly 'don't fight me on this one.' And if none of that explains it, I check whether this is a known provider bug for that resource type at my pinned version, because this exact symptom - identical diff reappearing after apply, console looks fine - is a recognizable pattern that shows up in provider issue trackers pretty often.

Uses ignore_changes as a blanket fix without confirming the attribute is genuinely externally managed
Doesn't consider checking for a known provider bug at the pinned version

questions.title: A Terraform Apply Failed Partway Through Creating a Multi-Resource Change
questions.prompt: A terraform apply that was creating five interdependent resources failed on the fourth, after successfully creating the first three. The error was a transient API timeout. Walk through how you'd safely get back to a clean, fully-applied state.
questions.modelAnswer: Terraform updates its state incrementally as each resource completes during an apply, not atomically at the very end, so the first three resources that succeeded are already correctly recorded in state, the fourth that failed mid-creation may or may not exist in the cloud depending on exactly when the timeout occurred, and the fifth was never attempted at all. The safe first step is simply running terraform plan again rather than assuming anything about what state things are in - the plan will show, based on the current state and current cloud reality, exactly what's left to do, which for a genuinely transient failure (an API timeout with no actual resource left in a broken state) is usually just 'create resource four and five,' identical to what the original plan intended for those two, since Terraform naturally picks up where it left off using the existing state rather than trying to recreate the already-successful first three. The one case requiring more care is if the failed resource partially created something in the cloud that Terraform's state doesn't know about - for example, a cloud resource that started provisioning and exists in a pending or partial state in the provider's console but isn't in Terraform's state at all because the create call never returned successfully - in which case a second terraform apply might try to create a duplicate and fail with a 'resource already exists' error, which would need to be resolved with a terraform import of the orphaned partial resource into state before retrying, rather than repeatedly reapplying against the same conflict.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing to remember is that Terraform writes to state as it goes, not all at once at the end, so those first three resources are already correctly recorded - this isn't a case where the whole apply needs to be treated as atomic or rolled back. My first move is just running plan again, not immediately reapplying, so I can see exactly what Terraform thinks is left to do based on current state and current reality. For a genuinely transient timeout with nothing actually left behind in a broken state, that plan usually just shows 'create resource four and five' and reapplying finishes the job cleanly, picking up right where it stopped. The case that actually needs real care is if that timeout happened after the cloud provider had already started creating the resource, just before the API call returned success back to Terraform - now there's a real resource sitting out there that Terraform's state has no idea exists. Reapplying blindly in that situation usually gets you a 'resource already exists' error, and the fix isn't to keep retrying the same apply, it's to find that orphaned resource and import it into state first, so Terraform and reality agree again before you try to move forward.

Doesn't run plan first to assess actual remaining work before reapplying
Doesn't consider the possibility of an orphaned, partially-created resource not yet in state

Proposes running plan first to assess the real remaining work
Identifies the orphaned-partial-resource edge case as requiring import
Avoids blind repeated reapplication in the face of a resource-exists conflict
