questions.title: A Pinned Module Version Broke a Build That Hadn't Changed
questions.prompt: A team's configuration pinned to a module version with '~> 2.0' suddenly started failing on a routine terraform init, with no changes to their own code. Walk through how you'd diagnose and fix this, and what it reveals about their version pinning.
questions.modelAnswer: The constraint '~> 2.0' is broader than it looks: depending on how many version components are specified, '~> 2.0' allows any 2.x release (2.1, 2.5, 2.9), not just 2.0.x patches, which is a very common misunderstanding of the ~> operator - '~> 2.0.0' would restrict to patch releases of 2.0.x only, while '~> 2.0' permits any minor version bump within major version 2. If the module author released a 2.x minor version that, despite semver intentions, introduced a behavior change or a bug, this team's unpinned-within-2.x constraint would pick it up automatically on the next init with no code change on their end at all, which is exactly what's being observed. The diagnosis is confirming the actual resolved module version via terraform init with verbose output or checking .terraform.lock.hcl / the module manifest for the version that was actually fetched, then checking that module's changelog for what changed between the previously working version and the newly resolved one. The immediate fix is tightening the constraint to the specific version that was previously known-good (or to '~> 2.0.0' for patch-only, if the team actually intended that narrower scope) to stop the bleeding, and separately, reviewing and deliberately adopting whatever changed in the new minor version on the team's own schedule rather than by accident. The broader lesson is that '~> 2.0' is often not what people think they're pinning to, and being explicit about intended scope (minor-locked vs. patch-locked) when writing the constraint avoids this exact surprise.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check is what '~> 2.0' actually allows, because this is one of the most common version-pinning misunderstandings I run into - that constraint permits any 2.x release, 2.1, 2.5, 2.9, not just patches within 2.0. If someone intended to lock to patches only, they needed '~> 2.0.0' with the extra zero, which is a meaningfully different, much narrower constraint. So what probably happened here is the module author shipped a 2.x minor release that changed something, even subtly, and this team's constraint happily picked it up on the next init with zero code changes on their end - which lines up exactly with what's being described. I'd confirm the actual resolved version from the lock file or verbose init output, then go read that module's changelog for whatever changed between the last known-good version and this one. The immediate fix is tightening the constraint back to the known-good version to stop anything else from moving underneath them, and then deliberately deciding, on their own timeline, whether to adopt whatever that new release changed. The real lesson I'd leave them with is to be explicit about whether they mean 'lock to this major' or 'lock to this exact minor, patches only' when they write the constraint, because '~> 2.0' quietly means the former even when people think they wrote the latter.

questions.title: An SLO Burn-Rate Alert Fires on a Metric Cardinality Explosion
questions.prompt: A burn-rate alert for a service's error budget starts firing constantly, but engineers investigating find no actual increase in real user-facing errors. Prometheus query performance has also degraded recently. Walk through what's likely happening and how you'd confirm and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: A false-positive burn-rate alert combined with degraded Prometheus query performance is the classic signature of a cardinality explosion - a label on the underlying metric (commonly something like a user ID, a raw request path with unbounded path parameters, or a trace/request ID mistakenly used as a label) is generating a huge and growing number of unique time series, which both slows down every query touching that metric (since Prometheus has to scan far more series than intended) and can distort an aggregate rate() calculation if the query's aggregation doesn't correctly collapse across the exploded label dimension, making a relatively small number of genuinely failing requests appear as a much larger proportion once sliced across thousands of near-unique label combinations with very low individual sample counts. The diagnostic step is checking Prometheus's own tsdb status or querying count by (__name__) (topk) style introspection to identify which specific metric and which specific label is responsible for the series count explosion, which usually points directly at the offending instrumentation point in the application code. The fix has two parts: immediately, relabeling or dropping the offending high-cardinality label at the scrape/relabel config level to stop the bleeding without needing an application redeploy, and durably, fixing the actual instrumentation to stop emitting that label at all (replacing a raw path with a normalized route template, removing a user ID label entirely) since relabeling at the Prometheus side is a stopgap, not a permanent fix for instrumentation that will keep generating the same problem elsewhere.
questions.professionalAnswer: False alerts plus slow Prometheus queries together is a pattern I recognize immediately - that's cardinality, almost always. Something, usually a label like a raw user ID, or a request path with an ID baked right into it instead of a normalized route template, is generating an explosion of unique time series, and that does two things at once: it slows every query touching that metric because Prometheus has way more series to scan than it should, and it can genuinely distort a rate calculation, making a handful of real failures look much bigger once they're sliced across thousands of near-empty label combinations. My first move is querying Prometheus's own series counts, usually some variant of counting by metric name and label, to find exactly which metric and which label is the culprit - that almost always points straight back to a specific line of instrumentation code. The immediate fix, the one that doesn't need a redeploy, is dropping or relabeling that specific label at the Prometheus scrape config level to stop the damage right now. But that's a stopgap, not the real fix - the actual fix is going back into the application and changing the instrumentation itself, usually swapping a raw path for a normalized route template, so it stops generating that cardinality in the first place. If I only fix it at the Prometheus side, the same mistake just shows up again the next time someone adds a similar metric.

Doesn't propose a concrete method for identifying the offending metric/label

questions.title: A Trace Shows High Latency but No Error, and Logs Show Nothing
questions.prompt: A distributed trace for a slow request shows most of the time sitting in a span for a downstream service call, but that service's own logs show nothing unusual and no errors. Walk through how you'd continue the investigation from here.
questions.modelAnswer: A span showing high duration with no corresponding error or anomaly in that service's application logs points away from application-level logic and toward something the application itself never logs because it isn't aware of it - most commonly time spent waiting rather than time spent computing. The next step is checking whether the span's duration actually represents the downstream service doing work, or time spent waiting to even start: a connection pool exhausted and queuing for an available connection, a thread pool saturated and queuing the request before it's even picked up, or DNS resolution and TCP/TLS handshake overhead on a cold connection, none of which necessarily produce an application log line because the application's own request-handling code hasn't started yet when that waiting happens. If the service exposes connection pool or queue depth metrics (a common gap - many services don't expose these by default), checking those metrics for the same time window as the slow trace would directly confirm or rule out a queuing cause. If tracing instrumentation only wraps the application's own handler and not the underlying HTTP client or database driver's connection acquisition step, the span itself may be mislabeled - attributing all of the latency to 'calling the downstream service' when a meaningful chunk is actually 'waiting for a connection to become available before the call could even start' - which means finer-grained instrumentation (a dedicated child span around connection acquisition specifically) may be needed to actually distinguish queuing time from genuine processing time within that single coarse span.
questions.professionalAnswer: A slow span with clean logs on the downstream side tells me the time is probably being spent somewhere the application itself never logs anything about, because it hasn't started doing application work yet - that's almost always some form of waiting rather than working. My next move is checking whether that span actually represents real processing time or queuing time - a connection pool with nothing free, a thread pool backed up, even just a cold connection eating DNS and TLS handshake time before a single line of application code runs. None of that produces an error log, because from the application's perspective nothing went wrong, it's just waiting its turn. If that service exposes connection pool or queue depth metrics - and a lot of services genuinely don't by default, which is itself worth flagging - I'd pull those for the exact same time window as the slow trace and see if there's a queuing spike that lines up. The other thing I check is whether the tracing instrumentation itself is coarse - if the span wraps the whole downstream call as one block instead of separately wrapping connection acquisition versus actual request processing, you can't actually tell queuing time apart from real work time just by looking at the one big span, and the fix there is adding a finer-grained child span specifically around connection acquisition so the next time this happens, the trace itself answers the question instead of requiring this whole investigation again.

questions.title: On-Call Is Being Paged Repeatedly for a Flapping Alert
questions.prompt: An on-call engineer is being paged every 15 minutes overnight by an alert that clears within a minute of firing each time, for a condition that's never actually required any manual intervention in months of history. Walk through how you'd fix this without just silencing the alert.
questions.modelAnswer: An alert that reliably clears within a minute and has never required manual intervention is, by definition, measuring a self-healing condition, and the fix is not to silence it (which would also hide the one future occasion it might actually matter) but to change what it's actually measuring or how it's evaluated so it only pages when the condition is genuinely sustained and actionable. The first check is whether the alert's for: duration is too short relative to the natural recovery time of whatever it's watching - if the underlying condition routinely self-resolves within 60-90 seconds, a for: of a few seconds or none at all means the alert fires on every brief blip; lengthening for: to comfortably exceed the typical self-healing window (say, 5 minutes) would stop it from paging on transient blips while still catching a genuinely sustained version of the same condition. The second check is whether the alert is measuring a cause (a specific metric crossing a threshold momentarily) rather than a symptom that actually matters to users, in which case the real fix is replacing this alert's condition entirely with one tied to actual user impact (an SLO burn rate, an actual error rate sustained over a window) rather than tuning the existing cause-based threshold. I'd also check the alert's history specifically for any night where it fired and genuinely should have paged, to make sure the retuning doesn't accidentally create a gap where a real incident goes unpaged - the goal is a correctly-tuned alert that pages only on genuine, sustained problems, not simply a quieter version of a fundamentally noisy one.
questions.professionalAnswer: An alert that always clears itself within a minute and has never once needed a human to fix anything is telling you clearly that it's watching something self-healing, not something broken - and silencing it is the wrong fix because the one time it actually matters, you've now turned it off. My first check is the for: duration relative to how fast this thing naturally recovers - if it self-resolves in under 90 seconds and the alert has no meaningful for: window, of course it's firing on every blip. Stretching for: out to comfortably outlast the normal self-healing time, five minutes say, means a genuinely brief blip never crosses the threshold to page, but a truly sustained version of the same condition still would. The deeper question I always ask, though, is whether this alert is watching a cause instead of a symptom that users actually feel - if it is, tuning the for: window is just a band-aid, and the real fix is retiring this alert entirely in favor of something tied to actual user-facing impact, like an SLO burn rate. Before I ship any of this, though, I go back through the alert's history specifically looking for any night it fired that genuinely should have paged someone, because the last thing I want is to quiet a noisy alert and accidentally create a blind spot for the one real incident buried in all that noise.

questions.title: A Security Scan Blocks a Release Over a Disputed False-Positive CVE
questions.prompt: A critical-severity CVE scan result is blocking a release, but the engineering team is confident it's a false positive - the vulnerable code path in the flagged library isn't actually reachable in how the application uses it. The release is time-sensitive. Walk through how you'd handle this without simply disabling the scanner.
questions.modelAnswer: The engineering team's confidence that a code path isn't reachable is a hypothesis, not a verified fact, and treating it as settled without verification is exactly how real vulnerabilities get waved through under release pressure, so the first step is actually confirming reachability rather than accepting the claim - checking whether the specific vulnerable function or code path in the flagged library is called anywhere in the application's actual call graph, which some SCA tools support directly (reachability analysis), or doing it manually by tracing the application's usage of that library's API surface. If reachability is genuinely confirmed as absent, the correct mechanism isn't disabling the scanner or the specific rule globally - it's a scoped, documented, time-boxed suppression for this specific CVE on this specific component, ideally supported natively by the scanning tool, with the suppression justification (the reachability analysis) recorded and attached to the suppression itself, visible to anyone auditing scan results later, and an expiration date forcing a re-review rather than a permanent, silent exception. If the analysis is inconclusive or the team's confidence doesn't hold up under actual scrutiny, the release should wait, or the team should take the smaller, faster fix of bumping the dependency to a patched version if one exists, which is almost always less work than a thorough reachability audit. The durable principle is that every exception needs documented justification and an expiration, because an organization that routinely accepts 'the team is confident it's fine' without verification will eventually ship a CVE that genuinely was reachable, waved through by the same unverified confidence.
questions.professionalAnswer: 'We're confident it's not reachable' is a claim I want verified, not accepted, because that exact sentence is how real vulnerabilities get shipped under deadline pressure. So before anything else, I'd actually check reachability - either with the scanner's own reachability analysis if it has one, or manually tracing whether the application's code ever actually calls into that vulnerable function at all. If that checks out and the path genuinely isn't reachable, the fix still isn't turning the scanner off or disabling that rule globally - it's a scoped suppression for this exact CVE on this exact component, with the reachability justification written down and attached to the suppression itself, and critically, an expiration date so this doesn't quietly become a permanent exception nobody revisits. If the reachability analysis is shaky or inconclusive, I'd push back on the release date rather than the scanner, or check if there's just a patched version available to bump to - that's usually faster than a real reachability audit anyway. The principle I hold the line on is that every exception needs a documented reason and a deadline to revisit it, because the first time 'the team is confident' gets accepted without verification and it turns out wrong, that's the incident that makes the case for why that principle existed in the first place.

questions.title: A Secrets Rotation Broke a Service Due to a Cached Credential
questions.prompt: A scheduled secrets rotation ran successfully and the secrets manager shows the new database credential as active, but a running service started failing authentication immediately after. Walk through how you'd diagnose and fix this, and how you'd prevent it on future rotations.
questions.modelAnswer: A rotation that succeeds at the secrets manager but breaks a running consumer is almost always a caching problem on the consumer side, not a rotation problem: the service likely read the credential once at startup and held it in memory (an environment variable set at container launch, a connection pool initialized once with the old password) with no mechanism to notice the secrets manager now has a new value, so from the service's perspective the credential it's using simply stopped working the moment the old one was invalidated or the database's own credential rotation took effect, even though the secrets manager was updated correctly. The diagnosis is confirming this by checking exactly when the service last actually fetched the secret versus when rotation occurred - if there's a gap of any meaningful length between 'service last read the secret' and 'rotation happened,' that confirms the caching theory rather than a rotation logic bug. The immediate fix is restarting the affected service (or its connection pool specifically, if that can be done without a full restart) so it picks up the current value, resolving the outage, but the durable fix requires the service to support dynamic credential refresh - either polling the secrets manager periodically, subscribing to a change notification if the secrets manager supports one, or at minimum a liveness-friendly way to force-refresh on an authentication failure rather than crash-looping - and the rotation process itself should include an overlap window (keeping the old credential valid for a defined grace period after the new one is issued) specifically to give every consumer, including ones with imperfect refresh logic, time to pick up the change before the old credential is hard-invalidated.
questions.professionalAnswer: A rotation that looks perfectly clean on the secrets manager side but breaks a running service is almost never a rotation bug - it's a caching problem on the consumer's side. That service almost certainly read the credential once, probably at startup, stuffed it into an environment variable or a connection pool, and has no idea the secrets manager has a new value now. From its perspective, the password it's holding just stopped working, and the timing lines up with the old credential getting invalidated, not with anything the service itself did wrong. I'd confirm that by checking when the service last actually fetched the secret versus when rotation ran - if there's any real gap there, that's the caching theory confirmed. The quick fix is just restarting the service, or its connection pool specifically if that's less disruptive, so it picks up the current value. But the fix that actually prevents this from happening again every rotation cycle is making the service support dynamic refresh - polling for the current secret periodically, or at minimum refreshing on an auth failure instead of just crash-looping. And on the rotation process side, I always push for an overlap window - keep the old credential valid for a defined grace period after the new one goes live, specifically so services that don't have perfect refresh logic still have time to catch up before the door actually closes on the old value.
commonMistakes: Assumes the rotation process itself is broken rather than suspecting consumer-side caching
Fixes the immediate outage with a restart but doesn't address the durable refresh gap
Doesn't propose an overlap/grace-period window for future rotations
Doesn't verify the diagnosis by checking the timing gap between last fetch and rotation

Proposes a concrete way to verify the diagnosis via fetch/rotation timing
Fixes the immediate outage and addresses the durable dynamic-refresh gap
Proposes an overlap/grace-period window for future rotations

Proposes a concrete verification method
Addresses both immediate fix and durable refresh capability

questions.title: Cluster Autoscaler Won't Scale Up Despite Pending Pods
questions.prompt: Several pods are stuck Pending for over ten minutes, clearly needing more capacity, but the Cluster Autoscaler isn't adding any nodes. Walk through the specific things you'd check, in order, to find out why.
questions.modelAnswer: The first check is the Cluster Autoscaler's own logs and events, which almost always state the specific reason directly rather than requiring guesswork - common root causes surface there explicitly. The most frequent cause is the node group already being at its configured maximum size, in which case Cluster Autoscaler is working correctly but is structurally prevented from adding capacity, and the fix is raising the max node count for that node group rather than debugging the autoscaler itself. A second common cause is the pending pod's resource requests not matching any available node group's instance type at all - if a pod requests more memory than the largest configured node type in any node group can provide, no amount of scaling helps, since Cluster Autoscaler only adds nodes of types already defined in existing node groups, it doesn't invent new node group configurations. A third cause is a pod-level scheduling constraint (a node selector, a taint the pod doesn't tolerate, a required anti-affinity rule) that makes the pod fundamentally unschedulable on any node Cluster Autoscaler could add, which Cluster Autoscaler is actually designed to detect and will note in its logs as 'no node group would help this pod,' correctly declining to scale up a node that wouldn't solve the problem anyway. A fourth, less common cause is a cloud-provider-level quota limit (a regional vCPU quota, for example) silently preventing new node provisioning even though Cluster Autoscaler is correctly attempting it, which shows up as a provisioning failure in cloud provider logs or events rather than in Cluster Autoscaler's own decision logic.
questions.professionalAnswer: Cluster Autoscaler's own logs are always my first stop, because it's usually pretty direct about why it isn't scaling, rather than something I have to reverse-engineer. The most common thing I find is the node group's already sitting at its configured max - the autoscaler isn't broken, it's correctly refusing to go past a limit someone set, and the fix is just raising that max, not debugging the tool. Second most common: the pending pod is asking for more resources than any configured node type in any node group could even provide - if nothing I've defined can fit this pod, scaling up more nodes of the same types doesn't help, Cluster Autoscaler can't invent a bigger instance type on its own. Third, and this one's actually by design, not a bug - if the pod has a node selector, an intolerable taint, or an anti-affinity rule that no addable node would satisfy anyway, Cluster Autoscaler is smart enough to recognize that scaling up wouldn't actually help this specific pod, and it logs exactly that and declines to add a useless node. Last thing I check, and it's the one people forget, is a cloud-provider-level quota - a regional vCPU limit, say - that's silently blocking new nodes from actually provisioning even though Cluster Autoscaler correctly tried, and that shows up in the cloud provider's own events, not in the autoscaler's decision logs.
commonMistakes: Doesn't check Cluster Autoscaler's own logs/events first before guessing at causes
Doesn't consider a node group already at its max size as a (correct, non-bug) explanation
Doesn't check whether the pod's resource request exceeds any available node type
Doesn't consider scheduling constraints (taints, affinity) or cloud-provider quota limits
keyPoints: Starts diagnosis with Cluster Autoscaler's own logs/events
Checks node group max-size limits as a common, correct-behavior cause
Checks whether pod resource requests exceed any available node type
Considers scheduling constraints and cloud-provider quota limits

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Starts with Cluster Autoscaler's own logs/events
Checks node group max-size limits
Checks resource request versus available node types
Considers scheduling constraints and quota limits

questions.title: Pods CrashLoopBackOff Only in Production After a Workload Identity Change
questions.prompt: After rolling out workload identity (federating pod service accounts to cloud IAM roles) across environments, pods in production go into CrashLoopBackOff immediately, while the identical deployment works fine in staging. Walk through how you'd diagnose this.
questions.modelAnswer: An identical deployment manifest behaving differently between environments means the difference is environmental, not in the application code or the manifest itself, so the investigation should start with kubectl logs and kubectl describe pod on the crashing production pod specifically, looking for an explicit authentication or permission error in the application's own startup logs - workload identity misconfigurations typically fail loudly at the exact point the application first tries to use a cloud SDK call, rather than failing silently. The most common environment-specific cause is that the cloud IAM role or trust policy bound to production's service account federation wasn't actually configured with the same permissions as staging's, or references the wrong cluster's OIDC issuer URL in its trust policy - since workload identity trust relationships are typically set up per-cluster, a trust policy copy-pasted from staging without updating the issuer URL to production's actual cluster would cause every token exchange to fail in production specifically, exactly matching the symptom. A second cause is a namespace or service-account-name mismatch - if the production namespace or service account name differs even slightly from what the trust policy or annotation expects (a common gap when environments aren't provisioned via identical, parameterized code), the federation silently fails to match. The fix starts with comparing the actual IAM trust policy and the Kubernetes service account annotation between the two environments line by line rather than assuming they're identical just because the deployment manifest is, since the workload identity configuration lives partly outside the deployment manifest itself (in IAM, and sometimes in a separate service account resource) and is exactly the kind of thing that's easy to configure correctly once and then not replicate precisely when standing up a new environment.
questions.professionalAnswer: Same manifest, different behavior between environments means the problem isn't in the manifest at all - it's in something environmental that the manifest doesn't capture. First thing I do is actually read the crashing pod's logs in production, because workload identity failures are usually loud, not silent - the app tries its first cloud SDK call and immediately gets an explicit auth error, which tells me a lot before I even start comparing configs. The most common thing I find in this exact scenario is that production's IAM trust policy either has different permissions than staging's, or - and this is the one I see most often - it's still referencing staging's cluster OIDC issuer URL because someone copy-pasted the trust policy and didn't update that one critical field for the new cluster. Trust relationships for workload identity are set up per-cluster, so that one missed field means every single token exchange in production fails, which matches this symptom exactly. The other thing I check is whether the service account name or namespace in production actually matches, character for character, what the trust policy or annotation expects - environments that aren't provisioned from the same parameterized code are exactly where this kind of tiny mismatch creeps in. I don't trust that the configs are identical just because the deployment YAML is - the workload identity wiring lives partly in IAM, outside the manifest entirely, and that's exactly the kind of thing that gets set up carefully once and then quietly not replicated when the next environment gets stood up.
commonMistakes: Debugs the application code or manifest instead of recognizing the problem is environmental
Doesn't start with the crashing pod's own logs for an explicit auth error
Doesn't check the IAM trust policy's OIDC issuer URL for a copy-paste mismatch between environments
Assumes the workload identity configuration is identical because the manifest is, without checking IAM directly
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the problem as environmental, not code/manifest-based
Starts diagnosis with the crashing pod's own logs
Checks the IAM trust policy's OIDC issuer URL for a per-cluster mismatch
Checks service account name/namespace matching between environments

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames this as an environmental, not code-level, problem
Starts diagnosis with pod logs for an explicit error
Checks the IAM trust policy/OIDC issuer for a per-cluster mismatch
Checks service account/namespace matching

questions.title: An Argo CD Application Stays OutOfSync After Manual Fixes
questions.prompt: An Argo CD Application shows 'OutOfSync' persistently, even right after someone manually edits the resource in the cluster to match what they believe Git describes. Walk through why this keeps happening and how you'd actually resolve it.
questions.modelAnswer: If selfHeal is enabled on this Application (which it should be for genuine GitOps), a manual edit to a resource Argo CD manages is, by design, not a fix at all - it's a drift event, and Argo CD will revert that manual change back to match Git on its next sync regardless of whether the manual edit happened to match what someone believed Git said, because Argo CD doesn't evaluate whether a manual change is 'correct,' it simply reconciles toward Git as the source of truth. This means the right diagnostic question isn't 'why does OutOfSync persist after my fix' but 'why does the live resource not actually match what's in Git,' and the actual mismatch is almost always between what the person believes is in the Git-tracked manifest/values file and what's genuinely committed there - checking the actual diff Argo CD's UI shows (not guessing) reveals specifically which fields disagree, which is frequently a values file that wasn't actually updated in the same commit the person assumes it was, a Helm chart default that differs from what's expected, or a webhook/annotation Argo CD itself injects that the person's manual edit doesn't account for. The correct fix is updating the actual source in Git to match the intended state and letting Argo CD sync from there, not editing the live cluster resource by hand at all, since any live edit - correct or not - is simply drift from Argo CD's perspective and will be treated accordingly on the next reconciliation.
questions.professionalAnswer: If selfHeal is on, which it should be for real GitOps, then a manual cluster edit was never actually a fix to begin with - it's drift, and Argo CD doesn't care whether the person believed their edit matched Git, it just reconciles back toward whatever Git actually says on the next sync. So the question to ask isn't 'why won't my fix stick,' it's 'why does the live resource not match Git in the first place.' I'd go look at the actual diff Argo CD's UI shows, field by field, instead of guessing, because that tells you exactly what disagrees - and in my experience it's almost always that the values file someone thinks got updated in a commit actually didn't, or there's a Helm default kicking in that nobody accounted for. The fix is never editing the live cluster resource by hand - that's the one thing guaranteed not to stick under selfHeal. The fix is updating the actual source file in Git to reflect the intended state and letting Argo CD sync from there normally. Once people internalize that any manual cluster edit is drift, full stop, regardless of whether it happens to be correct, this stops being confusing.
commonMistakes: Keeps manually editing the live resource, not recognizing it as drift under selfHeal
Doesn't check the actual diff Argo CD shows to identify what specifically disagrees
Assumes the problem is with Argo CD itself rather than a mismatch between Git and belief
Doesn't fix the actual source in Git before expecting the Application to sync cleanly
keyPoints: Correctly explains why manual cluster edits are treated as drift under selfHeal
Reframes the diagnostic question around what Git actually contains
Proposes checking Argo CD's own diff to identify the specific mismatch
Fixes the issue by updating Git, not the live cluster resource

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the selfHeal/drift behavior
Reframes the diagnosis toward the actual Git content
Proposes checking Argo CD's diff for the specific mismatch
Correctly fixes the issue via Git rather than the live cluster

questions.title: A Multi-Region Failover Didn't Work During a Real Outage
questions.prompt: During a real regional outage, an automated multi-region failover that had been tested successfully in drills did not actually redirect traffic, extending the incident significantly. Walk through how you'd investigate what went wrong, and what it reveals about the limits of drill-based testing.
questions.modelAnswer: The investigation should start by reconstructing the actual failover mechanism's decision path during the real incident minute-by-minute - what health check or signal was supposed to trigger failover, what that signal actually reported during the outage, and at what point (if any) the failover logic evaluated and declined to act - because 'the failover didn't work' usually decomposes into either 'the trigger condition was never actually met' or 'the trigger fired but the failover mechanism itself failed to execute,' and those have very different fixes. A common real-world gap is that failover drills are run as planned exercises that simulate the failure condition directly (manually flipping a flag, intentionally killing a specific service) rather than the actual messy failure mode a real regional outage produces, which might involve a partial, degraded failure (some services in the region still responding, just slowly, or a dependency the health check doesn't even monitor failing) that never crosses the specific binary threshold the automated trigger was built to detect - the health check says 'still healthy enough' right up until the incident is already severe, because the drill never tested a partial-degradation scenario, only a clean full-outage one. The postmortem needs to treat this as a testing methodology gap as much as a technical one: the durable fix is chaos-engineering-style fault injection that simulates partial, realistic degradation (latency injection, dependency failure, not just full service kill) rather than only clean binary failures, because a failover mechanism that's only ever been validated against the failure mode it was designed to detect will reliably fail against the failure mode reality actually produces, which is rarely that clean.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by reconstructing exactly what happened minute by minute during the real incident - what was the health check or signal actually reporting, and did the failover logic ever even evaluate and decide not to act, or did it never get triggered at all. Those are genuinely different problems with different fixes, and 'failover didn't work' as a one-line summary hides which one actually happened. What I usually find in situations like this is that the drills tested a clean, binary failure - someone flips a switch, a service goes fully down, failover triggers cleanly - and real outages are almost never that tidy. A real regional outage is often partial and degraded: some things still technically responding, just slow, or some dependency failing that the health check doesn't even look at, and the automated trigger's threshold never actually gets crossed because it was built to detect the clean failure, not this messy one. That's the real finding I'd push into the postmortem - this isn't just 'the failover had a bug,' it's that the testing methodology itself only ever validated against the failure mode it was designed to catch. The fix is bringing in real chaos-engineering-style fault injection - latency injection, partial dependency failure, not just a clean kill switch - because a failover that's only been tested against its own design assumptions is going to reliably miss whatever reality actually throws at it, which is rarely that clean.
commonMistakes: Treats 'failover didn't work' as a single fact rather than distinguishing trigger-never-fired from trigger-fired-but-execution-failed
Doesn't reconstruct the actual incident timeline against the failover's decision logic
Misses that drills testing clean/binary failure don't validate against realistic partial degradation
Proposes only a technical fix without addressing the testing methodology gap
keyPoints: Distinguishes trigger-never-met from trigger-fired-but-execution-failed
Reconstructs the actual incident timeline against the failover's decision path
Identifies the gap between clean drill scenarios and realistic partial degradation
Proposes chaos-engineering-style fault injection as the durable methodology fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the two failure categories
Proposes reconstructing the actual incident timeline
Identifies the drill-versus-reality testing gap
Proposes a durable fault-injection-based fix

questions.title: A Pipeline Passes Locally but Fails on Shared CI Runners Over Secret Scoping
questions.prompt: A team's deployment pipeline works perfectly when they test the same steps manually, but consistently fails with an authentication error when run through the organization's shared CI runners, which 40 other teams also use. Walk through how you'd diagnose this.
questions.modelAnswer: A step that authenticates fine manually but fails specifically when run through shared infrastructure almost always points at scoping - the secret or credential the step needs either isn't available in this pipeline's specific scope on the shared runner platform, or is available but with narrower permissions than what the person has personally when testing manually, which is a very common and easy-to-miss difference between an individual's own broad access and a pipeline's deliberately scoped service credential. On a shared runner platform serving 40 teams, secrets are typically scoped to a specific project, environment, or namespace for exactly this reason - to prevent one team's pipeline from being able to read another team's credentials - so the first check is confirming the secret this pipeline references is actually registered in the scope this specific pipeline runs under, not assuming it's globally available just because it exists somewhere in the organization's secrets store. A second common cause specific to shared runner environments is that the runner's own execution context (a service account or managed identity the CI platform itself assumes when running jobs) is what's actually making the authenticated call, not the human's personal credentials at all, and that service identity may have deliberately narrower permissions than an individual engineer - meaning the fix isn't 'use my credentials' but requesting the correct permission be granted to the pipeline's actual service identity. The fix should be verified by checking the CI platform's own logs for exactly which identity or secret reference was used for the failing call and what permission it actually had, rather than guessing from the pipeline YAML alone, since the YAML might reference a secret by name correctly while that secret is scoped somewhere the pipeline can't actually reach.
questions.professionalAnswer: Works manually, fails specifically on the shared runners - that pattern screams scoping to me before I even look at the YAML. The person's manual test is almost certainly running under their own, much broader personal credentials, and the pipeline on a shared runner serving 40 teams is running under something much narrower, usually a dedicated service identity the CI platform itself assumes, by design, specifically so one team's pipeline can't accidentally read another team's secrets. My first check is whether the secret this pipeline references is actually registered in the scope this specific pipeline runs in, not just somewhere in the org's secrets store generally - on a shared platform, that scoping is deliberate and strict. The other thing I check is what identity actually made the failing call - I pull the CI platform's own execution logs, not the YAML, because the YAML can reference a secret correctly by name while that secret sits in a scope the pipeline genuinely can't reach, and the logs tell me exactly which identity and which permission was actually in play at the moment it failed. The fix almost never is 'give the pipeline my credentials' - it's requesting the right permission be granted to the pipeline's own actual service identity, which is a very different, much safer conversation with whoever owns the shared runner platform.
commonMistakes: Assumes the pipeline YAML itself has a bug rather than suspecting a scoping mismatch
Doesn't distinguish the manual tester's personal credentials from the pipeline's service identity
Proposes granting the pipeline the engineer's own personal credentials as a fix
Doesn't check the CI platform's own execution logs to confirm which identity/secret was actually used
keyPoints: Correctly suspects secret/credential scoping as the root cause
Distinguishes personal credentials from the pipeline's own service identity
Proposes the correct fix: granting permission to the pipeline's service identity, not borrowing personal credentials
Verifies via CI platform execution logs rather than guessing from YAML alone

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses a scoping mismatch as the root cause
Distinguishes personal credentials from pipeline service identity
Proposes the correct, safe fix
Proposes verifying via CI platform logs

questions.title: A Monthly AWS Bill Shows a Huge, Unexplained Line Item With No Obvious Owner
questions.prompt: This month's AWS bill shows a large, unfamiliar charge under a service nobody remembers provisioning, and Cost Explorer's tag breakdown shows it as 'untagged.' Walk through exactly how you'd track down what it is, who owns it, and whether it should be decommissioned.
questions.modelAnswer: Since the cost allocation tag breakdown is unhelpful here (untagged), I'd go around it rather than through it: Cost Explorer's own 'Usage Type' and 'Linked Account' grouping (not just tags) will at minimum identify which account and which specific AWS service/usage type the charge belongs to, which narrows the search dramatically even with zero tags. From there, CloudTrail's event history (or, for older activity beyond its default retention, a configured CloudTrail trail with S3-archived logs) lets me search for the resource creation events for that service type in that account around when the charge started appearing, which typically reveals the IAM principal (user or role) that actually created it and the timestamp -- that's usually enough to identify an owner even when tags were never applied. If CloudTrail history doesn't reach back far enough, AWS Config (if enabled) maintains a configuration history and resource inventory that can also identify when a resource was created and its attributes. Once I have the resource identified and dated, I'd check whether it's still being used (CloudWatch utilization/access metrics for compute, access logs for storage, connection counts for databases) before concluding it's safe to decommission -- an untagged resource is often also an unmonitored one, and 'nobody remembers it' is not the same as 'nobody is using it'; I've seen untagged legacy resources turn out to be quietly load-bearing. Only after confirming genuine non-use (or getting explicit sign-off from whoever CloudTrail identifies as the creator, if they're still reachable) would I decommission it. The durable fix, regardless of what this specific resource turns out to be, is the SCP/tag-policy enforcement gap that let an untagged resource get created and run unnoticed long enough to generate a surprise bill line -- I'd flag that as the real finding to bring back to the team, not just 'we found and deleted one thing.'
questions.professionalAnswer: Tags being empty just means I go around them instead of through them. Cost Explorer's linked-account and usage-type breakdown still works without any tags, so that's my first stop to narrow down which account and which specific service this actually is. From there, CloudTrail is where I find out who actually created it -- searching resource-creation events for that service around when the charge first showed up usually surfaces the IAM principal and the exact timestamp, which gets me an owner even with zero tagging discipline on the resource itself. Before I touch anything, though, I want to know if it's actually being used right now -- untagged doesn't mean unused, and I've been burned before by assuming a forgotten-looking resource was dead when it was quietly serving something real. So I check utilization or access metrics first, and I'd try to actually reach whoever CloudTrail says created it before decommissioning anything. And honestly, the resource itself is almost the smaller story here -- the bigger finding I'd bring back to the team is that our tagging enforcement has a gap that let this run unnoticed long enough to show up as a surprise line item, and that's the thing actually worth fixing.
commonMistakes: Gives up on investigation because the cost allocation tag is empty, instead of using account/usage-type breakdown and CloudTrail
Decommissions the resource based on 'nobody remembers it' without checking actual usage/access metrics first
Doesn't use CloudTrail to identify the creating principal and timestamp
Treats this as a one-off cleanup without flagging the underlying tagging/governance gap
keyPoints: Uses Cost Explorer's account/usage-type grouping to narrow down the charge without relying on tags
Uses CloudTrail (and/or Config) to identify the creating principal and creation timestamp
Checks actual usage/access metrics before concluding a resource is safe to decommission
Flags the underlying tagging/governance gap as the real, durable finding

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sound investigation path despite missing tags
Correctly uses CloudTrail/Config to identify ownership
Verifies actual usage before recommending decommissioning
Identifies the governance gap as the durable finding

questions.title: Designing a Multi-Environment Terraform Promotion Architecture
questions.prompt: Design the full architecture for promoting infrastructure changes through dev, staging, and production using Terraform, including state organization, module sourcing, and policy enforcement, for a platform supporting 40 services.
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture has three layers working together. The module layer is a versioned, private registry of shared modules (networking, compute, database) that every environment's root configuration consumes by pinned version reference, so a module improvement is authored once and deliberately adopted by each environment on its own schedule rather than copy-pasted and diverging. The environment layer uses directory-per-environment root configurations, each with its own remote state file under a predictable key convention, each calling the shared modules with environment-specific variable files - this keeps dev, staging, and production fully independent in terms of blast radius while sharing the exact same underlying module logic, so a bug fixed in staging is the identical code that eventually reaches production, not a re-implementation. Promotion itself is a pull-request-driven workflow: a change lands first in the dev environment's directory, merges and applies automatically or on approval, then an explicit second pull request bumps staging's module version pins and variable file to match, and only after validation there does a third pull request promote the identical, already-validated configuration to production - each promotion step is its own reviewable, auditable change rather than a single change fanning out to all three environments at once. Policy as code sits in the pipeline between every environment's plan and apply, with policies tightening by environment - lenient in dev to avoid blocking experimentation, strict in production, catching a misconfiguration before it's created rather than after. State locking is backend-native at every tier, and remote state outputs (like a shared VPC ID from a networking state) are consumed via explicit data sources or a remote state data source reference rather than hardcoded values, keeping environments correctly decoupled while still able to reference each other's outputs where genuinely needed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I build this in three layers that reinforce each other. The module layer is a private registry - networking, compute, database, versioned properly - and every environment pulls those modules by a pinned version, so a fix gets written once and each environment chooses when to actually take it, rather than three slightly different copies of the same logic drifting apart over time. The environment layer is directory-per-environment, each with its own state, each calling the same shared modules with its own variables file - that's what keeps a bad apply in dev from ever touching staging or production, while guaranteeing all three are running the literal same module code, just at different adopted versions. Promotion is always a sequence of separate, reviewable pull requests - dev gets the change first, then a second PR bumps staging's pinned version to match and validates there, then a third PR promotes that exact same validated config to production. Nothing fans out to all three at once; each hop is its own auditable decision. Policy as code sits between plan and apply everywhere, but I tighten the rules by environment - dev stays loose so people can actually experiment, production is strict. And when one environment's config needs something from another, like a shared VPC ID, I pull that through an explicit remote state reference, never a hardcoded value, so the environments stay properly decoupled while still able to talk to each other where it's genuinely needed.
commonMistakes: Proposes a single shared configuration for all environments instead of directory-per-environment isolation
Doesn't version-pin shared modules, letting all environments silently track the same latest version
Fans a change out to all three environments in one step instead of sequential, reviewable promotion
Applies the same policy strictness to every environment instead of tightening toward production
Hardcodes cross-environment references instead of using remote state data sources

Uses directory-per-environment state isolation
Describes sequential, reviewable promotion through dev, staging, production
Applies policy as code with environment-appropriate strictness
Uses explicit remote state references for legitimate cross-environment dependencies

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a sound module versioning and registry layer
Designs sound environment/state isolation
Describes a correct sequential promotion workflow

questions.title: Designing State Segmentation for 200 Microservice Repositories
questions.prompt: Design a Terraform remote state segmentation strategy for a platform with over 200 independently-deployed microservice repositories, each needing its own infrastructure, plus shared infrastructure like networking and a container registry used by all of them.
questions.modelAnswer: The segmentation principle is matching state boundaries to deploy-independence and ownership: shared, rarely-changing infrastructure (the core VPC, the container registry, any central IAM/identity federation) lives in its own small number of foundational state files, owned and changed by the platform team, applied far less frequently and with heavier review given the blast radius of a mistake there. Each of the 200 services gets its own state file, scoped to exactly that service's resources, owned by that service's team, deployable independently without touching any other service's state or requiring coordination with 199 other teams. The connection between the two tiers is handled through remote state data sources or, more robustly at this scale, a small set of well-known outputs published from the foundational state (VPC ID, subnet IDs, registry URL) that service-level configurations read rather than each service re-deriving or hardcoding those values, which keeps foundational changes (like adding a new subnet) from requiring 200 separate service-level state files to be touched. Backend organization follows a predictable naming convention - a path like foundation/network.tfstate and services/<service-name>/<environment>.tfstate - generated through a standardized module or scaffolding tool rather than 200 teams each hand-rolling their own backend block, which is both an onboarding accelerant for new services and a consistency guarantee for encryption and locking configuration across all 200. I'd also add a lightweight registry or catalog of which state file corresponds to which service and owner, because at 200+ state files, 'who owns this state and what does it manage' becomes a real operational question that an ad hoc naming convention alone doesn't fully answer.
questions.professionalAnswer: At 200 services, the question I'm actually answering with state segmentation is 'can team 47 deploy without coordinating with the other 199 teams,' and the answer needs to be yes. So the shared stuff - core VPC, container registry, any central identity federation - lives in its own small number of foundational states, owned by the platform team, changed rarely and reviewed heavily because the blast radius there is genuinely large. Every one of the 200 services gets its own state, scoped tightly to just that service, owned by that service's team, deployable completely independently. The connection between those two tiers matters a lot at this scale - service configs read a handful of well-known outputs from the foundational state, like VPC ID or registry URL, through a remote state reference, rather than every service hardcoding values or trying to re-derive them, because otherwise a single new subnet added at the foundation level means touching 200 separate service configs instead of one. I always generate the backend configuration itself from a standard scaffolding tool rather than letting 200 teams hand-write their own backend blocks, partly for onboarding speed and partly because that's exactly where encryption or locking config quietly gets forgotten by team 150 if it's manual. And honestly, at this scale I also want a simple catalog - which state belongs to which service and who owns it - because 'what does this state file even manage' becomes a real question nobody can answer from memory once you're past a couple dozen states.

Doesn't separate foundational/shared infrastructure from per-service state
Has services hardcode shared infrastructure values instead of reading remote state outputs
Doesn't standardize backend configuration generation, leaving 200 teams to hand-roll their own
No catalog or registry of what each state file manages and who owns it
keyPoints: Separates foundational/shared state from per-service state
Scopes per-service state to enable fully independent deployment
Connects tiers via remote state outputs rather than hardcoding or duplication
Standardizes backend configuration generation across all 200 services
