evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates foundational from per-service state
Ensures per-service deployment independence
Connects tiers via remote state outputs appropriately
Standardizes backend configuration at scale
Addresses ownership/catalog tracking at this scale

questions.title: Designing an SLO and Shared On-Call Architecture Across Dozens of Services
questions.prompt: Design the SLO, error budget, and alerting architecture for a platform with 60 services owned by 12 teams, sharing a rotating on-call pool, where you need consistent reliability standards without forcing every team into identical, poorly-fitting SLOs.
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture needs a shared framework with team-specific parameters, not one-size-fits-all numbers: a standard SLI taxonomy (availability, latency, correctness) and a standard SLO template (how burn rate is calculated, how alerts are tiered) applied uniformly across all 60 services, but the specific SLO target and error budget for each service set by its owning team based on that service's actual criticality and realistic achievability, because a payment service and an internal reporting tool genuinely warrant different availability targets, and forcing both onto an identical 99.99% target either over-invests in the reporting tool's reliability or sets an unrealistic, demoralizing target the payment service's team didn't actually choose. Shared on-call across 12 teams for 60 services requires each service's alerts to carry enough embedded context (which team owns it, a direct runbook link, the specific SLO being threatened) that a rotating on-call engineer unfamiliar with a given service's internals can still triage effectively, since a shared rotation can't assume deep per-service knowledge the way a dedicated on-call for one team could. Escalation needs a tiered design: the rotating generalist on-call handles the first response and initial triage for everything, with an automatic escalation path to that specific service's actual owning team if the issue isn't resolved within a defined window, rather than expecting the generalist rotation to resolve every deep, service-specific issue alone. I'd centralize the tooling (one paging platform, one dashboard aggregating burn rate across all 60 services) while decentralizing the actual SLO targets and remediation ownership, which is the combination that scales governance without forcing uniformity that doesn't fit the platform's actual risk profile.
questions.professionalAnswer: What I don't do is hand all 60 services the same SLO number - a payment service and an internal reporting dashboard do not deserve the same 99.99% target, and forcing that either wastes serious engineering effort on the low-stakes service or sets an unrealistic bar the payment team never actually agreed to. What I do standardize is the framework - the same SLI categories, the same burn-rate math, the same alert tiering logic - applied consistently everywhere, while letting each owning team set their own actual target based on what that specific service's criticality really calls for. The harder design problem is the shared on-call rotation, because the person on call this week for 60 services they don't all know deeply still needs to triage effectively. That means every alert has to carry real context baked in - which team owns this, a direct runbook link, exactly which SLO is at risk - because I can't assume the rotating generalist has deep knowledge of any one of these 60 services the way a dedicated on-call would. Escalation has to be tiered too - the generalist handles first response and initial triage for everything, but there's an automatic, timed escalation path straight to the actual owning team if it's not resolved quickly, rather than expecting a generalist to solve every service's deep issue solo. The pattern that actually works is centralizing the tooling and the framework while decentralizing the actual targets and the remediation ownership.
commonMistakes: Forces identical SLO targets across all 60 services regardless of actual criticality
Doesn't address how a shared generalist rotation can effectively triage services they don't know deeply
Omits embedded alert context (ownership, runbooks, specific SLO) needed for unfamiliar on-call engineers
No tiered escalation path from generalist on-call to the actual owning team
Centralizes everything including SLO targets, producing a poor fit for differing service criticality
keyPoints: Standardizes the SLO/SLI framework while letting teams set their own targets
Addresses how a shared rotation triages unfamiliar services via embedded alert context
Designs a tiered escalation path to the actual owning team
Centralizes tooling/framework while decentralizing targets and remediation ownership

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly balances standardized framework with team-specific targets
Addresses shared-rotation triage via embedded alert context
Designs a sound tiered escalation path
Articulates the centralize-tooling/decentralize-targets pattern

questions.title: Designing a Distributed Tracing Architecture Across Polyglot Services
questions.prompt: Design a distributed tracing architecture for a platform with services written in four different languages, deployed across Kubernetes and a few legacy VMs, aiming for consistent trace coverage without requiring every team to hand-roll their own instrumentation.
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture centers on OpenTelemetry specifically because it's vendor-neutral and has mature SDKs across all major languages, which matters directly for a four-language polyglot estate - standardizing on OpenTelemetry avoids locking the tracing layer to whichever backend is chosen today, and lets teams in different languages all emit a consistent trace format without each adopting a different, language-specific proprietary agent. For instrumentation coverage without per-team hand-rolling, I'd push auto-instrumentation libraries (available for most common frameworks across the four languages) as the default, covering HTTP, database, and messaging calls automatically, reserving manual span creation for business-logic-specific spans teams actually want visibility into beyond what auto-instrumentation captures. The collection architecture uses the OpenTelemetry Collector deployed as a sidecar or per-node agent in Kubernetes (via a DaemonSet) for low-latency local collection, with legacy VMs running a standalone Collector instance or forwarding directly to a centrally-deployed Collector gateway, which then handles sampling, batching, and resource enrichment centrally before exporting to the tracing backend - this means sampling policy and backend choice can change centrally without redeploying instrumentation across four languages and two infrastructure types. The critical cross-cutting requirement, given the mixed infrastructure, is consistent context propagation: every service-to-service call, regardless of language or whether it crosses from Kubernetes to a legacy VM, must correctly forward W3C Trace Context headers, which means any internal HTTP client library or message queue wrapper used across the four languages needs to be verified (and if necessary patched) to propagate those headers, since a single non-propagating hop anywhere in the service graph fractures every trace that passes through it.
questions.professionalAnswer: OpenTelemetry is the obvious backbone here specifically because of the four-language problem - it's vendor-neutral with solid SDKs across all the major languages, so I'm not locking the tracing layer to whatever backend we pick today, and every team emits the same trace format regardless of what language they're in. For actual coverage without making 12 teams hand-instrument everything themselves, auto-instrumentation is the default - it covers HTTP, database, and messaging calls automatically for most common frameworks, and I only ask teams to add manual spans for business logic they specifically want visibility into beyond what auto-instrumentation already gives them for free. On the collection side, Kubernetes gets the OpenTelemetry Collector as a DaemonSet for fast local collection, and the legacy VMs either run their own standalone Collector or forward straight to a central gateway Collector - that central point is where I handle sampling and enrichment policy, specifically so I can change sampling rates or swap the backend later without touching instrumentation in four different languages across two totally different infrastructure types. The thing I watch most carefully given this mixed VM-plus-Kubernetes setup is context propagation - every single hop, no matter the language, no matter whether it's crossing from a pod to a legacy VM, has to correctly carry the W3C trace context headers forward. I'd actually audit every internal HTTP client and message queue wrapper in use across all four languages for this, because one hop anywhere that drops those headers breaks every single trace that happens to pass through it.
commonMistakes: Proposes a vendor-specific or single-language tracing agent instead of a vendor-neutral standard like OpenTelemetry
Requires manual instrumentation everywhere instead of defaulting to auto-instrumentation
Doesn't address collection architecture differences between Kubernetes and legacy VMs
Doesn't address context propagation consistency across languages and infrastructure types as the critical risk
keyPoints: Chooses a vendor-neutral, multi-language standard (OpenTelemetry)
Defaults to auto-instrumentation to avoid per-team manual effort
Designs appropriate collection architecture for both Kubernetes and legacy VMs
Identifies cross-language, cross-infrastructure context propagation as the critical risk to verify

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly chooses and justifies a vendor-neutral tracing standard
Designs sound instrumentation coverage strategy
Designs appropriate collection architecture across mixed infrastructure
Identifies and addresses context propagation risk

questions.title: Designing a Shift-Left Security Pipeline Architecture for Many Teams
questions.prompt: Design the security gates and tooling architecture for a CI/CD platform shared by 25 teams, covering SAST, dependency scanning, secrets detection, IaC scanning, and image scanning, as a shared, governed pipeline-as-code standard.
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture needs each scanning category wired into a shared pipeline template, not reimplemented per team, with each category's gate placed at the earliest point it can actually run: secrets detection and SAST run on every pull request since both are fast and don't require a built artifact; dependency/composition scanning also runs on pull request against the manifest, catching a known-vulnerable library before merge; IaC scanning runs specifically on any pull request touching Terraform or similar configuration, evaluating the plan rather than raw HCL; image scanning runs after build, once an actual image artifact exists to scan, both in CI before push and continuously against the registry afterward. Governance comes from making these gates part of the shared pipeline-as-code template that all 25 teams consume by reference, the same architecture used for CI/CD platform governance generally - a team opting out means visibly not using the shared template, which is a reviewable deviation, rather than a silently missing scan step in a bespoke pipeline. Each gate's block-versus-warn policy needs to be tuned by severity and fixability rather than uniformly strict, since a blanket block-everything policy across 25 teams' worth of legacy code and dependencies would generate enough false-positive friction to get the whole program abandoned within months; findings with no available fix get tracked against a remediation SLA rather than blocking. Centralized dashboards aggregating findings across all 25 teams give the security team platform-wide visibility without needing to chase each team individually, while each team's own pipeline failures stay local and actionable to just that team. Rollout itself should be staged - running every gate in warn-only mode first across all teams to establish a baseline and avoid breaking everyone simultaneously, then flipping to blocking mode team by team as their backlog of pre-existing findings gets triaged down to a manageable level.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wire every scanning category into one shared pipeline template that all 25 teams consume by reference, and I place each gate at the earliest point it can actually run usefully. Secrets detection and SAST go on every pull request, no built artifact needed, both are fast. Dependency scanning runs against the manifest on PR too, catching a known-bad library before merge. IaC scanning runs specifically against the plan output, on any PR touching infrastructure config. Image scanning has to wait until there's an actual image, so that's post-build, both in CI and then continuously against the registry afterward. The governance piece is the same pattern I use for any shared pipeline standard - these gates live inside the shared template itself, so skipping one means visibly not using the shared template at all, which somebody notices, rather than a scan step quietly missing from one team's bespoke YAML. I'm careful about block-versus-warn policy here too - a blanket 'block on everything' across 25 teams' worth of accumulated legacy findings would generate so much false-positive friction that the whole program gets quietly abandoned within a quarter. Findings with no fix available get tracked against an SLA instead of blocking anyone. And I always roll this out staged - every gate goes in warn-only first, across all 25 teams, so we get a real baseline without breaking anyone's Friday deploy, and only flips to actually blocking team by team once their existing backlog is triaged down to something manageable.
commonMistakes: Doesn't place each scanning category at the correct, earliest-possible point in the pipeline
Lets each team reimplement security gates independently instead of a shared, governed template
Proposes a uniform block-everything policy without considering severity/fixability tuning
No staged rollout plan, risking breaking all 25 teams simultaneously
keyPoints: Correctly places each scanning category at its earliest viable pipeline point
Governs via a shared pipeline-as-code template rather than per-team reimplementation
Tunes block-vs-warn policy by severity and fixability
Proposes a staged, warn-then-block rollout across teams

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly places each security gate in the pipeline
Designs sound shared-template governance
Designs a sustainable block-vs-warn policy
Proposes a realistic staged rollout

questions.title: Designing Secrets Management Architecture With No Static Long-Lived Secrets
questions.prompt: Design a secrets management architecture for a platform spanning Kubernetes, serverless functions, and CI/CD pipelines, with a hard requirement that there are no static, long-lived credentials anywhere in the system.
questions.modelAnswer: Eliminating static long-lived secrets means every consumer needs a path to a dynamically-issued, short-lived credential rather than a pre-provisioned password or API key, and the mechanism differs by consumer type but shares one underlying pattern: establish trust via workload identity (an OIDC-federated identity the platform already vouches for) and exchange that trust for a short-lived credential on demand. For Kubernetes workloads, this means Kubernetes service account token federation (via the cluster's OIDC issuer) trusted by Vault or the cloud provider's own identity federation, letting a pod exchange its own Kubernetes-issued identity token for a short-lived cloud credential or a dynamically-generated database credential with a TTL, with no static secret ever stored in a Kubernetes Secret object at rest. For serverless functions, the cloud provider's own execution role (an IAM role attached to the function, assumed automatically at invocation) plays the same role - the function never holds a static credential, it holds an identity the cloud platform itself vouches for and exchanges for temporary credentials transparently. For CI/CD pipelines, OIDC federation between the CI platform and the cloud provider (GitHub Actions' or a similar platform's OIDC token exchanged for a short-lived cloud role) replaces long-lived CI-stored API keys entirely. The remaining hard case is systems that genuinely can't support any form of workload identity federation (some legacy or third-party systems) - for those, Vault's dynamic secrets engine generates a credential on demand with a short lease specifically for that system, which isn't zero-static-secret in the purest sense but minimizes the exposure window dramatically compared to a credential that's manually created once and never rotated. The architecture's single point of trust becomes the identity federation configuration itself (which OIDC issuers are trusted, by which roles), which needs to be the most tightly controlled and audited piece of the entire system, since compromising that trust relationship would undermine every credential issued through it.
questions.professionalAnswer: Getting rid of static long-lived secrets means every single consumer needs some path to a short-lived, dynamically issued credential instead of a password sitting around forever, and the mechanism changes by consumer type but the underlying idea is always the same - establish trust through workload identity, then trade that trust for a short-lived credential right when it's needed. For Kubernetes, that's federating the cluster's own OIDC issuer so a pod's Kubernetes-issued identity token can be exchanged for a short-lived cloud credential or a Vault-generated database credential with a real TTL - nothing static sits in a Kubernetes Secret object. For serverless, the cloud's own execution role does the same job automatically - the function never holds a credential at all, it holds an identity the platform vouches for and silently exchanges for temporary access. For CI/CD, OIDC federation between the CI platform and the cloud replaces the long-lived API key that used to sit in CI secrets forever. The genuinely hard case is some legacy or third-party system that just can't do any of this federation - for those, Vault's dynamic secrets engine generating something on demand with a short lease is the best available answer, and while that's not technically zero static secrets, it shrinks the exposure window enormously compared to a credential someone created once and forgot about. The piece I'd actually lose sleep over here is the identity federation trust configuration itself - which issuers are trusted, by which roles - because that single configuration is now effectively the root of trust for every credential the whole system ever issues, and it needs to be the most locked-down, most audited thing in the entire architecture.
commonMistakes: Proposes rotating static secrets more frequently instead of eliminating them via dynamic issuance
Doesn't address the different mechanism needed for Kubernetes, serverless, and CI/CD separately
Doesn't acknowledge the legacy/third-party system edge case or propose a reasonable fallback
Doesn't identify the identity federation trust configuration itself as the new critical control point
keyPoints: Correctly uses workload identity federation as the underlying pattern across consumer types
Addresses Kubernetes, serverless, and CI/CD with appropriate, distinct mechanisms
Proposes a reasonable fallback (Vault dynamic secrets) for systems that can't federate
Identifies identity federation trust configuration as the new critical control point

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly applies workload identity federation as the core pattern
Addresses all three consumer types with correct, distinct mechanisms
Proposes a sound fallback for non-federatable systems
Identifies the trust configuration as the critical control point

questions.title: Designing a Multi-Cluster Kubernetes Strategy for Regional Disaster Recovery
questions.prompt: Design a multi-cluster Kubernetes strategy spanning two cloud regions for disaster recovery, including your choice between active-active and active-passive, and how application state, traffic routing, and cluster configuration stay consistent across both clusters.
questions.modelAnswer: Active-active (both regions serving live traffic simultaneously) delivers lower recovery time (there's no failover delay since both regions are already handling real traffic) but requires the application and its data layer to genuinely tolerate multi-region writes or careful data partitioning, which is a significant application-level constraint many systems don't actually meet; active-passive (one region live, the second provisioned and synced but not serving traffic until failover) is simpler to reason about for data consistency since only one region writes at a time, at the cost of a failover delay and the real risk that a passive region which hasn't actually served production traffic recently has configuration or capacity drift nobody would notice until the moment it's actually needed. Given that risk, I'd recommend active-passive with a regularly scheduled, automated failover drill (not just a provisioned-and-forgotten passive cluster) specifically to catch that drift before a real disaster does, unless the application's data layer genuinely supports multi-region writes, in which case active-active's lower recovery time is worth the added complexity. Cluster configuration consistency across both clusters is solved with GitOps as the actual mechanism, not a policy ask - both clusters run an Argo CD or Flux instance syncing from the same Git source, so a configuration change merged once is automatically applied identically to both clusters, and selfHeal prevents either cluster from silently drifting from the shared source over time. Traffic routing uses DNS-based or global load balancer failover (health-checking the active region and redirecting to the passive region on failure) with a deliberately short TTL to minimize the propagation delay during an actual failover event. For data, the honest answer depends entirely on the data layer's actual replication capability - I'd design around whatever consistency guarantees the database genuinely provides rather than assuming synchronous cross-region replication is free or instant, since that assumption is one of the most common reasons DR plans fail during a real regional outage.
questions.professionalAnswer: Active-active sounds better on paper because there's no failover delay, both regions are already live - but it demands that your application and its data layer genuinely tolerate multi-region writes or careful partitioning, and a lot of systems just don't actually meet that bar even when people assume they do. Active-passive is simpler to reason about because only one region is writing at any given time, but it comes with a real, specific risk - a passive region that hasn't served real traffic in months can quietly drift in config or capacity, and nobody finds out until the actual disaster, which is the worst possible moment to discover it. So unless the data layer genuinely supports multi-region writes, I go active-passive, but I pair it with a real, scheduled, automated failover drill - not a provisioned-and-forgotten standby - specifically to catch that drift before reality does. Keeping both clusters' configuration consistent isn't a policy I write down and hope people follow, it's GitOps as the actual mechanism - both clusters run Argo CD or Flux syncing from the same Git source, with selfHeal on, so a config change merged once lands identically on both, and neither cluster can silently drift from what Git says. Traffic routing is DNS or global load balancer failover with a short TTL specifically to minimize how long it takes for traffic to actually move during a real event. And on data, I'm honest that the whole plan lives or dies on whatever the database's actual replication guarantees are - assuming synchronous cross-region replication is instant and free is probably the single most common reason DR plans fail the one time they're actually needed.
commonMistakes: Recommends active-active without addressing the data-layer multi-region write requirement
Proposes a passive cluster with no regular failover drill, risking undetected drift
Doesn't propose GitOps (or an equivalent concrete mechanism) for cross-cluster configuration consistency
Assumes cross-region data replication is instant/free without justifying against the actual database's guarantees
keyPoints: Correctly weighs active-active versus active-passive tradeoffs
Proposes regular, automated failover drills to catch passive-region drift
Uses GitOps as the concrete mechanism for cross-cluster configuration consistency
Grounds the data/replication plan in the actual database's real guarantees

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly analyzes active-active vs. active-passive tradeoffs
Proposes drilling/testing to catch passive-region drift
Proposes a concrete configuration consistency mechanism (GitOps)
Grounds data consistency plan in real replication guarantees
